blocks.text: Wrap the grocery assistant in an API: one SSE streaming endpoint, JWT auth, per-user rate limit, idempotency key on "place order", and a background job for document ingestion.

blocks.title: Design the backend for a streaming chat assistant in a mobile app, from tap to last token.
blocks.text: App sends the message with a JWT to POST /assistant/messages. Backend verifies the token, checks per-user token and spend limits, loads history, builds the prompt with a stable cached prefix, and opens a streaming model call with a timeout. It maps provider events to its own SSE events, cancels upstream if the client disconnects, validates and stores the final message with usage and cost, and emits a done event. Tools run server-side with the user id from the token and idempotency keys on writes.

modules.title: M4 · Retrieval foundations
modules.summary: The journey built a small semantic search and one RAG assistant. This module opens the box: how similarity search stays fast at a million chunks, and why keyword search still earns its place.

blocks.text: An embedding model turns a piece of text into a fixed-length vector so that texts with similar meaning land near each other. It is a separate, much smaller model than the chat model.
How it behaves

Choose by retrieval benchmark on your own data, dimension count (storage and speed), maximum input length and language coverage. Many models are asymmetric: queries and documents are embedded with different instructions or prefixes. Some support shortening the vector with little loss (Matryoshka embeddings). Changing the embedding model means re-embedding the whole corpus, so store the model name and version with every vector.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Embedding queries and documents with different models, or forgetting the query/document prefix the model expects. Scores look plausible and retrieval is quietly poor.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: text → embedding model → vector (e.g. 1024 numbers) → normalise → store with model version

blocks.title: What forces you to re-embed your entire corpus, and how do you make that survivable?
blocks.text: Changing the embedding model or its version, because vectors from different models are not comparable. Store the model id with each vector, build the new index alongside the old, evaluate recall on a golden set, then switch reads over and delete the old one.
Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors: 1 means same direction, 0 unrelated. It ignores the vectors' magnitude and compares direction only.
How it behaves

If vectors are normalised to length 1, cosine, dot product and Euclidean distance all give the same ranking, and dot product is the cheapest. Scores are only comparable within one model; 0.78 is not "78% relevant", and a fixed threshold tuned on one model is wrong on another.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: A hard-coded cut-off like "score > 0.8" copied from a blog post. Calibrate thresholds on your own labelled pairs.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: query vector · chunk vector → divide by lengths → score → sort descending → top k

blocks.title: When are cosine similarity and dot product equivalent?
blocks.text: When all vectors are normalised to unit length. Then the denominator is 1, the two give identical rankings, and you can use the faster inner-product index operator.
Chunking splits documents into the units you embed and retrieve. A chunk must be small enough to be about one thing and large enough to make sense alone.
How it behaves

Order of preference: split on the document's own structure (headings, list items, table rows, functions), then fall back to recursive splitting on paragraphs and sentences with a size limit and a small overlap. Carry the heading path and document title into each chunk. Fixed-size character windows are the baseline to beat, not the goal. The right size is found by evaluating retrieval, commonly a few hundred tokens.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Splitting a table or a numbered procedure across chunks, so no single chunk contains the answer.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: parsed document → split on structure → too big? split on paragraphs/sentences → add overlap + heading path → chunks

blocks.title: How do you decide chunk size?
blocks.text: Empirically. Build a small golden set of questions with the passages that answer them, index at two or three sizes, and compare recall@k and answer quality. Start from structural units and a few hundred tokens rather than a fixed character count.
A vector database stores vectors with their text and metadata and answers "which stored vectors are nearest to this one" quickly using an approximate index.
How it behaves

The options are an extension to a database you already run (pgvector), a dedicated engine (Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus, Pinecone), or a search engine with vector support (OpenSearch, Elasticsearch). Compare on filtered-search behaviour, hybrid search support, update cost, multi-tenancy and operations, not on headline speed. Exact brute-force search is fine up to tens of thousands of vectors.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Adopting a dedicated vector service for 20,000 chunks, then maintaining two sources of truth that drift.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: chunks + vectors + metadata → ANN index → query vector + filter → nearest k ids → fetch text

blocks.title: When is a dedicated vector database justified over pgvector?
blocks.text: When measured needs exceed what Postgres gives: very large corpora, high query rates with strict latency, heavy filtered search, or built-in hybrid and multi-tenant features you would otherwise build. Until then, one database is simpler and transactionally consistent.
pgvector is a Postgres extension that adds a `vector` column type, distance operators and approximate indexes. Your chunks, metadata and embeddings live in one table and one transaction.
How it behaves

Operators: `<=>` cosine distance, `<#>` negative inner product, `<->` Euclidean. Index types are HNSW (better recall and speed, more memory, slower build) and IVFFlat (cheaper, needs training data and tuning). The index must be built with the operator class that matches the operator in your query, or it will not be used. Combine with ordinary `WHERE` clauses and Postgres full-text search for hybrid.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Creating the index with `vector_l2_ops` and querying with `<=>`. The query silently does a full scan.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: CREATE EXTENSION vector → embedding vector(n) column → HNSW index with matching ops → ORDER BY embedding <= → $1 LIMIT k

blocks.title: Your pgvector query is slow even though an HNSW index exists. What do you check first?
blocks.text: Run EXPLAIN. The usual causes are an operator that does not match the index's operator class, a filter that makes the planner abandon the index, or a missing LIMIT / ORDER BY in the form the index supports.

HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is a layered graph. Each vector is linked to its near neighbours; upper layers have few nodes and long links, lower layers have all nodes and short links. Search starts at the top and greedily walks towards the query.
How it behaves

Three knobs: `M` (links per node: more recall, more memory), `ef_construction` (build effort) and `ef_search` (candidates explored per query: more recall, more latency). It is approximate, so some true neighbours are missed; measure recall against exact search on a sample. It needs to fit in memory to be fast, and inserts are relatively expensive. In pgvector, `hnsw.ef_search` (default 40) also caps how many rows one index scan can return.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Tuning for speed without ever measuring recall. You can make search very fast by making it wrong.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: query → enter top layer → greedy hop to closer neighbour → drop a layer → repeat → bottom layer: best ef_search candidates → top k

blocks.title: What do M and ef_search control in HNSW, and how do you tune them?
blocks.text: M sets how many links each node keeps, trading memory and build time for recall. ef_search sets how many candidates a query explores, trading latency for recall. Compare against exact search on sample queries and raise ef_search until recall meets your target.
Each chunk carries metadata such as tenant, document type, language, date, product. Filtering restricts the search to chunks that are allowed and relevant before similarity is considered.
How it behaves

Filter placement matters. Post-filtering (search then discard) can return fewer than k or nothing when the filter is selective. Pre-filtering is exact but may bypass the vector index. Good engines filter during graph traversal. Filters can be set by code from the session (tenant, permissions) or extracted from the question by a model ("returns policy from 2026" → year = 2026).

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Post-filtering by tenant: the top 10 nearest chunks all belong to other tenants and the user gets an empty result.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: query → filters from session + extracted from question → filtered ANN search → top k allowed chunks

blocks.title: Why is post-filtering dangerous with a selective filter?
blocks.text: The index returns the k nearest overall, then the filter removes most of them, leaving few or zero results even though matching chunks exist. Use filtered search inside the index, or over-fetch heavily and verify result counts.
BM25 scores a document by the query words it contains: rare words count more, repeated words count with diminishing returns, and long documents are normalised down.
How it behaves

Two parameters: `k1` (how fast repetition saturates) and `b` (how strongly to normalise by length). It is unbeatable on exact identifiers that embeddings blur: SKUs, order numbers, error codes, names, version strings. It has no notion of synonyms. In Postgres use full-text search or a BM25 extension; in search engines it is the default ranking.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Dropping keyword search because "embeddings understand meaning". Then a search for "SKU 40021873" returns chunks about SKUs in general.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: tokenise query → for each term: inverse document frequency × saturated term frequency → sum → rank

blocks.title: Give two query types where BM25 beats vector search and two where it loses.
blocks.text: BM25 wins on exact tokens (product codes, error strings, rare names) and when the user quotes the document's wording. It loses on paraphrases and synonyms ("money back" vs "refund") and on cross-language queries.
Hybrid search runs keyword and vector retrieval side by side and merges the two ranked lists, so you get exact matches and meaning matches.
How it behaves

The scores are on different scales, so merge by rank, not by score. Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) gives each document 1/(k + rank) from each list, with k around 60, and sums them. It needs no tuning and is hard to beat. A weighted fusion can help once you have an eval set to tune on.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Adding a BM25 score of 14.2 to a cosine score of 0.81 and calling it hybrid.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: query → BM25 top N + vector top N (in parallel) → reciprocal rank fusion → merged top k → reranker

blocks.title: Explain reciprocal rank fusion and why it is preferred over adding scores.
blocks.text: Each list contributes 1/(k + rank) per document and the contributions are summed. It uses only ranks, so it is unaffected by the two retrievers' incompatible score scales, and a document ranked well by both rises to the top.

A reranker is a cross-encoder: it reads the query and one candidate chunk together and outputs a relevance score. It is far more accurate than comparing two separately computed vectors, and far slower.
How it behaves

Hence two stages: cheap retrieval fetches 50 to 100 candidates for recall, the reranker reorders them for precision, and you pass the best 3 to 8 to the model. It adds tens to hundreds of milliseconds. Options are hosted rerank APIs, open cross-encoder models, or an LLM asked to rank. A reranker cannot recover a passage the first stage never returned.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Reranking the top 5. The right passage was at rank 23 and never reached the reranker.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: retrieve top 50–100 (recall) → cross-encoder scores each (query, chunk) pair → sort → keep top 3–8 → LLM

blocks.title: Why not use a cross-encoder for the whole corpus instead of embeddings?
blocks.text: It must run once per query-document pair, so a million chunks means a million model passes per query. Embeddings are computed once per document offline. Use the cheap method to shortlist and the expensive one to order the shortlist.

lessons.title: Go deeper: one query through the whole retriever

blocks.text: Go deeper: one query through the whole retriever
The ten topics above are stages of one pipeline. Follow a single question through it: a customer of tenant 42 asks "can I return opened milk?"

rows: tenant id and permissions come from the session, not the question
filter applied after the search instead of inside it
the question becomes a vector from the same model that indexed the documents, with that model's query prefix (documents got its document prefix)
wrong model version, or missing prefix
HNSW walks its graph for the nearest chunks, and the tenant filter is applied to what the walk returns
low search effort, so true neighbours are missed or too few rows survive the filter
full-text search returns the 50 best word matches
tokenizer splits codes; a query that requires every word matches nothing
reciprocal rank fusion merges the two lists by rank
adding raw scores from two different scales
a cross-encoder reads question and chunk together, reorders the top 40
reranking too few, so the right chunk never reaches it
the best 5 go to the model with their ids
passing 20 "to be safe", burying the answer

blocks.text: Every stage has a number you can measure. Module 5 gives you the metrics; this section gives you the mechanics.
Chunking decides what can be found

Chunking is usually blamed last and guilty first. The example splits one short policy three ways and asks two things of each: is every answer sentence whole inside one chunk, and does the chunk say what it is about?

blocks.code:
# Three ways to chunk the same policy. Check: does one chunk hold each full answer, and does it say what it is about?
DOC = """# Returns policy
## Fresh produce
Fresh produce can be returned at the door if it is damaged. The delivery partner will record it in the app.
## Dairy and frozen
Dairy and frozen items must be reported within 24 hours of delivery with a photo of the pack. Opened packs are accepted if the item was spoiled on arrival.
## Refunds
Refunds go to the original payment method within five working days. Wallet refunds are instant."""

ANSWERS = ["Dairy and frozen items must be reported within 24 hours of delivery with a photo of the pack.",
           "Opened packs are accepted if the item was spoiled on arrival.",
           "Refunds go to the original payment method within five working days."]


def fixed(text, size=18):
    w = text.replace("#", "").split()
    return [" ".join(w[i:i + size]) for i in range(0, len(w), size)]


def by_sentence(text):
    body = " ".join(l for l in text.split("\n") if not l.startswith("#"))
    return [s.strip() + "." for s in body.split(".") if s.strip()]


def by_heading(text):
    chunks, title, section = [], "", ""
    for line in text.split("\n"):
        if line.startswith("# "): title = line[2:]
        elif line.startswith("## "): section = line[3:]
        else: chunks.append(f"[{title} > {section}] {line}")       # heading path travels with the chunk
    return chunks


for name, chunks in [("fixed 18 words", fixed(DOC)), ("one sentence each", by_sentence(DOC)), ("by heading, with path", by_heading(DOC))]:
    whole = sum(any(a in c for c in chunks) for a in ANSWERS)
    labelled = sum(any(a in c and "Dairy" in c.split("]")[0] for c in chunks) for a in ANSWERS[:2])
    sizes = [len(c.split()) for c in chunks]
    print(f"{name:22} {len(chunks)} chunks, {min(sizes)}-{max(sizes)} words   answers kept whole {whole}/3   dairy answers that say 'dairy' {labelled}/2")
print("\n'Opened packs are accepted...' never says dairy. Only the heading path lets a search for dairy find it.")
blocks.caption: Fixed windows, single sentences and heading-aware chunks on the same document

blocks.text: The second dairy rule, "Opened packs are accepted if the item was spoiled on arrival", never contains the word dairy. Split by sentence, it is a correct chunk that no dairy question will retrieve. Carrying the heading path into each chunk fixes that at no model cost, and Module 5's contextual retrieval is the stronger version of the same idea.
The table and the indexes, in SQL

This is a complete pgvector setup for hybrid search with tenant isolation. Every statement was executed on 12 November 2026 against Postgres 16 with pgvector 0.8.0, on 4,000 test rows with random vectors. That proves the statements run and behave as described; it says nothing about speed or quality on your data. On a table that small the planner prefers an exact scan, so check your own plans with `EXPLAIN`.
The vector search. `<=>` is cosine distance, so smaller is closer and the ordering is ascending.

blocks.code:
SET hnsw.ef_search = 100;                -- search effort for this session
SET hnsw.iterative_scan = strict_order;  -- pgvector 0.8+: keep walking until LIMIT rows pass the filter

SELECT id, body, embedding <=> $1 AS distance
FROM chunks
WHERE tenant_id = $2
ORDER BY embedding <=> $1
LIMIT 50;

blocks.text: Hybrid search with rank fusion in one statement. Each side produces a rank; the outer query adds 1 / (60 + rank).

blocks.code:
WITH kw AS (
  SELECT id, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY ts_rank_cd(tsv, q) DESC) AS r
  FROM chunks,
       to_tsquery('english',
         replace(websearch_to_tsquery('english', $3)::text, ' & ', ' | ')) AS q
  WHERE tenant_id = $2 AND tsv @@ q
  ORDER BY ts_rank_cd(tsv, q) DESC
  LIMIT 50
), vec AS (
  SELECT id, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY embedding <=> $1) AS r
  FROM chunks
  WHERE tenant_id = $2
  ORDER BY embedding <=> $1
  LIMIT 50
)
SELECT id, sum(1.0 / (60 + r)) AS score
FROM (SELECT * FROM kw UNION ALL SELECT * FROM vec) AS both_lists
GROUP BY id
ORDER BY score DESC
LIMIT 40;

items: Postgres's built-in `ts_rank_cd` is a keyword ranking but not BM25. It is good enough to start; a BM25 extension or a search engine is the upgrade if keyword quality matters.

An HNSW scan filters after the walk. In the test run, a tenant owning 2% of the rows got 2 rows back for `LIMIT 50` when the index was used without iterative scan, and all 50 with it. The setting needs pgvector 0.8 or later.

`websearch_to_tsquery` requires every word of the question to be present, which a natural question almost never satisfies. The `replace` turns its ANDs into ORs so that any word can match and the ranking does the sorting.
The heading is part of `tsv`, so a chunk can be found by its section title. Build the embedding from heading plus body for the same reason.
The operator class must match the operator. In the test run an index built with `vector_l2_ops` was ignored by a `<=>` query, which fell back to a full scan.

Store `embed_model` on every row so you always know what made a vector. Running two models side by side takes more than the label: a second column or table for the new vectors, or partial indexes per model, because one index must hold vectors from one model only.

blocks.text: HNSW: the dial between speed and recall

An HNSW index is a graph of points linked to their neighbours. A search walks it greedily, keeping the best `ef_search` candidates seen so far. This toy builds the bottom layer of such a graph and measures what the dial does. Real HNSW adds sparse upper layers that act as a fast entry ramp; the trade-off below is the same.

blocks.code:
# The bottom layer of HNSW as a toy: a neighbour graph, greedy search, and recall versus ef_search.
import heapq, math, random

random.seed(4)
N, M, EF_BUILD, K, DIM = 1500, 4, 12, 10, 16
rand_vec = lambda: tuple(random.gauss(0, 1) for _ in range(DIM))
pts = [rand_vec() for _ in range(N)]
dist = lambda a, b: math.dist(a, b)
links = {i: [] for i in range(N)}


def search(q, ef, entry=0, upto=None):
    """Best-first walk over the graph. Returns (nearest ids, number of distance computations)."""
    seen, computed = {entry}, 1
    d0 = dist(q, pts[entry])
    frontier, best = [(d0, entry)], [(-d0, entry)]          # min-heap to expand, max-heap of the ef best so far
    while frontier:
        d, node = heapq.heappop(frontier)
        if d > -best[0][0] and len(best) >= ef:
            break                                           # nothing closer left to expand
        for nb in links[node]:
            if nb in seen or (upto is not None and nb >= upto):
                continue
            seen.add(nb); computed += 1
            dn = dist(q, pts[nb])
            if len(best) < ef or dn < -best[0][0]:
                heapq.heappush(frontier, (dn, nb)); heapq.heappush(best, (-dn, nb))
                if len(best) > ef:
                    heapq.heappop(best)
    return [i for _, i in sorted((-d, i) for d, i in best)], computed


for i in range(1, N):                                       # build: link each new point to its M nearest found
    near, _ = search(pts[i], EF_BUILD, upto=i)
    for nb in near[:M]:
        links[i].append(nb); links[nb].append(i)
        if len(links[nb]) > 2 * M:                          # keep the closest 2M links only
            links[nb] = sorted(links[nb], key=lambda j: dist(pts[nb], pts[j]))[:2 * M]

queries = [rand_vec() for _ in range(200)]
truth = [set(sorted(range(N), key=lambda i: dist(q, pts[i]))[:K]) for q in queries]
print(f"{N} points in {DIM} dimensions, up to {2 * M} links each. Exact search computes {N} distances per query.")
print("ef_search  recall@10  distances computed")
for ef in (10, 20, 40, 80, 160, 320):
    hit = comp = 0
    for q, t in zip(queries, truth):
        found, c = search(q, ef)
        hit += len(t & set(found[:K])); comp += c
    den = K * len(queries)
    tenths = (2000 * hit + den) // (2 * den)        # recall in tenths of a percent, rounded half up
    print(f"{ef:>9}  {str(tenths // 10) + '.' + str(tenths % 10) + '%':>9}  {comp / len(queries):>10.0f}")
blocks.caption: 1,500 points in 16 dimensions: recall and work at six settings of ef_search

blocks.text: At the lowest setting the search does a twentieth of the work of an exact scan and finds fewer than half of the true neighbours. Each doubling of effort buys less recall than the last. Nothing in your application errors when recall is 44%: results still come back, they are just the wrong ones. That is why recall has to be measured against exact search on a sample, and why "the vector database is fast" says nothing by itself.
Filters: inside the search or after it
Tenant isolation is the filter that must never fail. This example gives one tenant 2% of the index and compares filtering after the search with filtering inside it.

blocks.code:
# Post-filter versus filtered search when one tenant owns a small share of the index.
import math, random

random.seed(11)
N, K = 5000, 10
rows = [{"id": i, "tenant": "small" if random.random() < 0.02 else "big", "v": (random.random(), random.random())} for i in range(N)]
mine = [r for r in rows if r["tenant"] == "small"]
print(f"{N} chunks, {len(mine)} belong to this tenant ({len(mine) / N:.1%})\n")


def nearest(q, pool, k):
    return sorted(pool, key=lambda r: math.dist(q, r["v"]))[:k]


queries = [(random.random(), random.random()) for _ in range(300)]
print("strategy                         avg results   queries with fewer than 10   queries with none")
for label, fetch in [("post-filter, fetch 10", 10), ("post-filter, fetch 100", 100), ("post-filter, fetch 500", 500), ("filter inside the search", None)]:
    counts = []
    for q in queries:
        if fetch is None:
            got = nearest(q, mine, K)
        else:
            got = [r for r in nearest(q, rows, fetch) if r["tenant"] == "small"][:K]
        counts.append(len(got))
    print(f"{label:30} {sum(counts) / len(counts):>10.1f} {sum(c < K for c in counts) / len(counts):>22.0%} {sum(c == 0 for c in counts) / len(counts):>22.0%}")
blocks.caption: The same 300 queries under four filtering strategies

blocks.text: Fetching the top 10 and then filtering returns nothing four times out of five. Fetching 500 still falls short of 10 results on a quarter of queries, at fifty times the work. Filtering inside the search always returns 10. For a hard boundary such as tenant or permissions, use an engine and query shape that filter during the search, or give large tenants their own partition.
Which retriever fails on which question

blocks.text: What people get wrong about this module

items: "Vector search understands meaning, so keyword search is obsolete." Embeddings blur exactly the tokens users type most precisely: codes, names, numbers.
"A similarity of 0.8 means 80% relevant." Scores are only comparable within one model, and their range differs by model.
"The index returns the nearest neighbours." It returns approximately the nearest. How approximately is a setting you chose.
"Bigger chunks give more context, so they are safer." They embed to a vaguer meaning and fill the prompt with unrelated text.
"We filter by tenant, so it is isolated." Only if the filter is inside the retrieval query and in every cache key.
"A reranker fixes bad retrieval." It reorders what was retrieved. It cannot add what was missed.

blocks.text: Practice: five problems

blocks.title: Compute the cosine similarity of a = (3, 4) and b = (4, 3). Then say what it would be after both are normalised to length 1, and what the dot product of the normalised vectors is.
blocks.text: a · b = 12 + 12 = 24. Both lengths are 5, so cosine = 24 ÷ 25 = 0.96. Normalising does not change the angle, so cosine stays 0.96, and the dot product of the unit vectors is also 0.96. That equality is why normalised vectors let you use the cheaper inner-product operator.

blocks.title: Keyword search ranks documents A, B, C. Vector search ranks C, D, A. Using reciprocal rank fusion with k = 60, what is the fused order?
blocks.text: A: 1/61 + 1/63 = 0.03227. C: 1/63 + 1/61 = 0.03227. B: 1/62 = 0.01613. D: 1/62 = 0.01613. A and C tie at the top because each is first in one list and third in the other; B and D tie below. Documents found by both retrievers beat documents found by one, which is the point of fusion.

blocks.title: You plan to index 2 million chunks with 1,024-dimension embeddings stored as 4-byte floats. How much memory do the raw vectors need, and what changes if you use a 256-dimension version of the same model?
blocks.text: 2,000,000 × 1,024 × 4 bytes = 8.2 GB for vectors alone, before the HNSW graph, which adds its links on top. At 256 dimensions it is 2.05 GB, a quarter. Whether the shorter vectors are acceptable is an empirical question: measure recall on your golden set at both sizes.

blocks.title: A tenant owns 2% of the chunks. You search the whole index for the top 100 and then keep only that tenant's rows. How many results do you expect, and how many would you need to fetch to expect 10?
blocks.text: 100 × 0.02 = 2 results on average. To expect 10 you would fetch 500, and because that is only an average, a good share of queries would still return fewer than 10. Filter inside the search instead.

blocks.title: Retrieval returns 50 candidates and a cross-encoder scores one query-chunk pair in 4 milliseconds when run one at a time, or a batch of 50 in 60 milliseconds. Your retrieval budget is 300 milliseconds and search takes 80. What do you do?
blocks.text: One at a time is 200 ms, leaving 20 ms of slack; batched is 60 ms, leaving 160 ms. Batch the pairs in one call. With the remaining budget you could rerank 100 candidates for better recall into the reranker, or keep the headroom for the slow requests at p95.
Your retrieval design sheet
The build step moves the index into Postgres. Fill this in before writing code, and keep it beside the SQL; Module 5's evals will test every row.

blocks.title: Search works for "how do I get my money back" but fails for "error E-4012 at checkout". Diagnose and fix.
blocks.text: The first is a paraphrase that embeddings handle. The second hinges on an exact token that embeddings blur. Add keyword search and fuse with RRF, make sure the tokenizer keeps codes like E-4012 intact, and add exact-identifier queries to the eval set.

blocks.title: Design retrieval for 2 million support articles across 300 tenants with a 300 ms budget.
blocks.text: Postgres or a search engine with tenant-filtered HNSW and full-text indexes, both queried in parallel with the tenant id from the session. Fetch 50 from each, fuse with RRF, rerank the top 40 with a fast cross-encoder, return 6. Cache query embeddings, measure recall@k and p95 per stage, and partition or shard by tenant if large tenants dominate.

modules.title: M5 · Advanced RAG and measuring retrieval
modules.summary: Most RAG failures are retrieval failures. These ten techniques each fix a specific one, and the metrics tell you which one you have.

blocks.text: Parsing turns PDFs, Word files, HTML, slides and scans into clean structured text. Whatever is lost here cannot be retrieved later.
How it behaves

Hard parts: multi-column reading order, tables, headers and footers repeated on every page, scanned pages needing OCR, and figures. Keep structure (headings, lists, tables as Markdown or HTML) and page numbers for citations. Options range from text-layer extraction, to layout-aware parsers, to sending page images to a vision model for difficult pages. Mix them: cheap path first, vision model only where the cheap path fails a quality check.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Judging the RAG system by its answers without ever opening the parsed text. Garbled tables and merged columns are invisible until you look.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: file → detect type → extract text + layout → tables to Markdown → strip headers/footers → keep page numbers → structured document

blocks.title: Answers about a pricing table are wrong, although the PDF is indexed. Where do you look first?
blocks.text: At the parsed chunk for that table. Tables often come out as a run of numbers with rows and columns lost. Fix parsing (layout-aware extraction or a vision model for that page) and keep each table whole with its caption.
Index small chunks for precise matching, but hand the model the larger parent section they came from. Small units match queries well; large units give enough context to answer.
How it behaves

Store each child with its parent id. Search over children, then replace hits with their parents and de-duplicate when several children share one. The "sentence window" variant returns the matched sentence plus neighbours. Watch the token budget: five parents can be ten times larger than five children.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Returning five full parents for five children of the same section and filling the context with one section five times.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: section (parent) → split into small children → embed children → match child → fetch its parent → de-duplicate → LLM

blocks.title: What problem does parent-child chunking solve?
blocks.text: The tension between retrieval precision and answer context. Small chunks embed to a focused meaning and match well, but lack surrounding detail. Retrieving by child and returning the parent gives both.

A chunk taken alone often loses what it is about ("the limit is 7 days" — limit of what?). Contextual retrieval prepends a short generated sentence that situates each chunk in its document before embedding and keyword-indexing it.
How it behaves

At index time, a model is given the whole document plus one chunk and writes one or two sentences of context ("From the returns policy for perishable goods, section on refund windows"). Prompt caching makes this affordable because the document is the cached prefix across all its chunks. Anthropic's published results reported large drops in retrieval failures, especially combined with BM25 and reranking. A cheaper version prepends the title and heading path with no model call.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Running it without caching the document prefix, paying for the full document once per chunk.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: document (cached) + chunk → model writes 1–2 sentence context → context + chunk → embed and BM25-index

blocks.title: How is contextual retrieval different from adding chunk overlap?
blocks.text: Overlap repeats neighbouring text and only helps at boundaries. Contextual retrieval adds document-level information the chunk never contained, such as which product or policy it belongs to, so both embedding and keyword search can match on it.
Users' questions are often poor search queries: follow-ups with pronouns, several questions in one, or vague wording. Query rewriting uses a model to produce better queries before retrieval.
How it behaves

Three forms. Condense: turn "and for frozen items?" plus the history into a standalone question. Decompose: split a multi-part question into sub-queries, retrieve for each, and merge. Expand: generate a few paraphrases and fuse the results. Each adds a model call, so use a small fast model and only when needed.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Sending the raw follow-up "what about the second one?" to the vector index.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: conversation + latest message → small model rewrites to standalone query (or several) → retrieve for each → fuse

blocks.title: Retrieval is good on the first turn and poor on follow-ups. Why and what is the fix?
blocks.text: Follow-ups depend on earlier turns ("it", "that one"), so embedding them alone loses the subject. Rewrite each turn into a standalone query using the conversation before retrieving.

HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings) asks a model to write a plausible answer to the question first, then embeds that answer and searches with it. An answer resembles the documents more than a question does.
How it behaves

It helps when queries are short and documents are long and formal, and with general-purpose embedding models on unfamiliar domains. The generated answer may contain wrong facts, but it is only used as a search probe and thrown away. It costs one generation per query and can drag retrieval off course when the model's guess is far from your domain.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Showing or reusing the hypothetical answer. It is a search key, not content.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: question → model writes hypothetical answer → embed that → search → real chunks → answer from real chunks

blocks.title: Why can embedding a made-up answer retrieve better than embedding the question?
blocks.text: Questions and answers are phrased differently and sit in different regions of embedding space. A hypothetical answer uses the vocabulary and form of real documents, so its nearest neighbours are more likely to be the passages that answer the question.
A citation ties each claim in the answer to the exact passage that supports it, so the user can check and you can measure grounding.
How it behaves

Give each chunk an id, ask for the supporting quote before the claim, and return structured citations (chunk id, quote, character range). Then verify in code that every quoted span really appears in the cited chunk and drop or flag anything that does not. Some provider APIs return citations natively with guaranteed valid spans. Render them as tappable sources in the app.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Asking for "sources" and getting a tidy list of invented document titles.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: chunks with ids → model answers with quote + id per claim → code checks quote is in that chunk → render linked sources

blocks.title: How do you stop a RAG assistant from citing sources that do not support its claim?
blocks.text: Require a verbatim quote with a chunk id for each claim, verify in code that the quote occurs in that chunk, and reject or regenerate claims that fail. Measure with a faithfulness eval rather than trusting the format.
Recall@k asks: of the passages that should have been found, what fraction appear in the top k results? It is the first number to check in any RAG system.
How it behaves

You need a labelled set: questions paired with the ids of passages that answer them. If the right passage is not in the top k, no prompt can fix the answer. Report it at the k you actually pass to the reranker and at the k you pass to the model. Hit rate@k is the simpler variant: was at least one correct passage in the top k.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Tuning the generation prompt for a week when recall@5 was 55% all along.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: golden questions with relevant ids → run retriever → top k ids → relevant found ÷ relevant total → average over questions

blocks.title: An answer is wrong. How do you decide whether retrieval or generation is at fault?
blocks.text: Check whether the passage containing the answer was in the context sent to the model. If not, it is a retrieval failure (measure recall@k). If it was there and the answer is still wrong, it is a generation failure (measure faithfulness).

Both score the order of results. MRR (mean reciprocal rank) is 1/rank of the first relevant result, averaged. nDCG (normalised discounted cumulative gain) rewards putting more relevant results higher, with graded relevance and a log discount by position.
How it behaves

Use MRR when one correct passage is enough (FAQ lookup). Use nDCG when several passages matter and some are better than others. Recall tells you if the passage was found; these tell you if it was ranked where the model will use it. A reranker should raise nDCG without changing recall of its input set.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Reporting only recall@20 while passing the top 5 to the model.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: ranked results + relevance labels → MRR: 1 ÷ rank of first hit → nDCG: Σ gain ÷ log2(rank+1) ÷ ideal → average

blocks.title: You add a reranker. Which metric should move and which should not?
blocks.text: nDCG and MRR at small k should rise, because relevant passages move up. Recall over the candidate set stays the same, since a reranker only reorders what retrieval already returned.

GraphRAG builds a knowledge graph from the corpus (entities and relationships extracted by a model), groups it into communities and pre-writes summaries of each. Queries can then follow relationships or use summaries instead of matching isolated chunks.
How it behaves

It answers what plain vector search cannot: multi-hop questions ("which suppliers are affected by the policy that changed after the March incident") and corpus-wide questions ("what are the main complaint themes"). The cost is heavy: many model calls at index time, a graph to maintain when documents change, and extraction errors that compound.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Building a graph for a FAQ corpus where every question is answered by one passage.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: documents → extract entities + relations → graph → cluster into communities → summarise each → query: local (walk neighbours) or global (summaries)

blocks.title: Which questions justify GraphRAG over hybrid search with reranking?
blocks.text: Questions that need connecting facts across documents (multi-hop) or summarising the whole corpus. For single-passage factual lookups it adds cost and failure modes without gain. Prove the need with eval questions that plain RAG fails.
In agentic RAG the model holds search as a tool and decides whether to search, what to search for, whether the results are good enough, and whether to search again.
How it behaves

This replaces the fixed retrieve-then-answer pipeline with a loop. It handles multi-step and ambiguous questions and can pick between sources (policy index, order database, web). It costs more calls and latency and can loop, so cap the number of searches and require an answer or an explicit "not found". Most coding agents work this way, using grep and file reads rather than embeddings.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Making every question agentic. A one-hop FAQ answer now takes four model calls instead of one.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: question → model: need to search? → search tool → judge results → enough? no: refine query and search again → yes: answer with citations

blocks.title: When is a fixed retrieve-then-generate pipeline better than agentic RAG?
blocks.text: When questions are single-hop, latency and cost matter, and behaviour must be predictable. One retrieval and one generation is faster, cheaper and easier to evaluate. Add the loop only for question types the pipeline measurably fails.

lessons.title: Go deeper: pick the technique from the failure

blocks.text: Go deeper: pick the technique from the failure

Module 4 built the retriever. This module is ten ways to improve one, and the mistake to avoid is adding them because they exist. Each one answers a specific failure, and each has a price. Find the failure first.

blocks.text: If you cannot say which row you are in, you need the metrics below before any technique.
An ablation: one change at a time

This is the working method for the whole module. Keep the golden questions fixed, change one thing, measure, keep or revert. The corpus is ten policy chunks; three of the eight questions are follow-ups with no subject, the way real users type them.

blocks.code:
# An ablation: change one thing at a time and measure retrieval on the same golden questions.
# Retrieval here is TF-IDF cosine from the standard library; the method is the same with real embeddings.
import math
from collections import Counter

CHUNKS = [   # (id, heading path, body)
    ("c1", "Returns > Fresh produce", "Can be returned at the door if damaged. The delivery partner records it in the app."),
    ("c2", "Returns > Dairy and frozen", "Must be reported within 24 hours of delivery with a photo of the pack."),
    ("c3", "Returns > Dairy and frozen", "Opened packs are accepted if the item was spoiled on arrival."),
    ("c4", "Returns > Packaged groceries", "Can be returned within seven days if the pack is unopened."),
    ("c5", "Refunds > Timing", "Money goes back to the original payment method within five working days."),
    ("c6", "Refunds > Wallet", "Credits to the app wallet are instant."),
    ("c7", "Delivery > Slots", "A slot can be changed up to one hour before dispatch."),
    ("c8", "Delivery > Fees", "Orders above 499 rupees have no delivery fee."),
    ("c9", "Delivery > Missed delivery", "If nobody is at home the partner waits ten minutes and then leaves."),
    ("c10", "Account > Clearance items", "Items bought on clearance cannot be returned unless unsafe to eat."),
]
GOLDEN = [   # (question as typed, standalone rewrite a small model would produce, id of the chunk that answers it)
    ("how long do I have to report spoiled dairy", None, "c2"),
    ("can I return opened frozen food", None, "c3"),
    ("when do I get my refund", None, "c5"),
    ("is the wallet refund faster", None, "c6"),
    ("can I move my delivery slot", None, "c7"),
    ("what about unopened ones?", "can I return unopened packaged groceries", "c4"),
    ("can those be returned too?", "can clearance items be returned", "c10"),
    ("is there a charge for that?", "is there a delivery fee on my order", "c8"),
]
STOP = set("a an the is are do i my to of for if it be can and what how when have about there on in at that those too ones".split())
words = lambda s: [w for w in s.lower().replace("?", "").replace(".", "").replace(">", " ").split() if w not in STOP]


def build(texts):
    df = Counter(w for t in texts.values() for w in set(words(t)))
    idf = {w: math.log(len(texts) / n) + 1 for w, n in df.items()}
    vec = lambda s: {w: c * idf.get(w, 0) for w, c in Counter(words(s)).items()}
    return {i: vec(t) for i, t in texts.items()}, vec


def cosine(a, b):
    dot = sum(v * b.get(w, 0) for w, v in a.items())
    na, nb = math.sqrt(sum(v * v for v in a.values())), math.sqrt(sum(v * v for v in b.values()))
    return dot / (na * nb) if na and nb else 0.0


def evaluate(index_text, use_rewrite):
    index, vec = build(index_text)
    hit1 = hit3 = rr = 0
    for typed, rewrite, answer in GOLDEN:
        q = vec(rewrite if (use_rewrite and rewrite) else typed)
        ranked = sorted(index, key=lambda i: -cosine(q, index[i]))
        rank = ranked.index(answer) + 1
        hit1 += rank == 1; hit3 += rank <= 3; rr += 1 / rank
    n = len(GOLDEN)
    return hit1 / n, hit3 / n, rr / n


body_only = {i: b for i, _, b in CHUNKS}
with_heading = {i: f"{h} {b}" for i, h, b in CHUNKS}
print(f"{'configuration':44} recall@1  recall@3  MRR")
for label, index_text, rewrite in [("baseline: chunk body only", body_only, False),
                                   ("+ heading path indexed with each chunk", with_heading, False),
                                   ("+ follow-ups rewritten to standalone", with_heading, True),
                                   ("rewrite only, no heading path", body_only, True)]:
    r1, r3, mrr = evaluate(index_text, rewrite)
    print(f"{label:44} {r1:>7.0%}  {r3:>8.0%}  {mrr:.2f}")
blocks.caption: Four configurations measured on the same eight questions

blocks.text: Three lessons are in that table. Rewriting follow-ups was the change that mattered here; indexing the heading path barely moved the numbers, although it is cheap and you would keep it. You could not have known that order without measuring. And after both changes one question still fails: "when do I get my refund" matches no chunk at all (a score of zero against every one, so its rank is an arbitrary tie), because the chunk says "money goes back" and the heading says "Refunds", plural. That is a vocabulary mismatch, the failure that embeddings and HyDE exist for, and you only find it by reading the question that failed.
The two prompts worth knowing

Contextual retrieval and HyDE are each one short prompt. For contextual retrieval the whole document goes first so it can be cached, then one chunk; the model's one or two sentences are prepended to the chunk before it is embedded and keyword-indexed.

blocks.code:
<document>
{the full document, identical for every chunk of it, cached}
</document>

Here is one chunk from that document:
<chunk>
{chunk text}
</chunk>

Write one or two sentences that place this chunk within the document,
naming the product, policy or section it belongs to, so that a search
can find it. Reply with only those sentences.

blocks.text: For HyDE the model writes a plausible answer, and you embed that answer to search with. The answer is never shown and never trusted.

blocks.code:
Write a short passage that would answer the question below, in the
style of a company policy document. It will be used only as a search
query, so plausible wording matters more than being right.

Question: {user question}

blocks.text: Both add model calls, so both go through the ablation before they stay.
Parent-child, and the duplicate you must remove
Small pieces match precisely; sections answer fully. This example retrieves by sentence and then returns sections.

blocks.code:
# Parent-child retrieval: match on small pieces, hand the model the section they came from, once.
SECTIONS = {
    "S1 Dairy and frozen": ["Must be reported within 24 hours of delivery.", "A photo of the pack is required.",
                            "Opened packs are accepted if the item was spoiled on arrival.", "Refunds follow the standard timing."],
    "S2 Packaged groceries": ["Can be returned within seven days.", "The pack must be unopened.", "Bring the invoice."],
    "S3 Refund timing": ["Money goes back to the original payment method.", "This takes five working days.", "Wallet credits are instant."],
}
children = [(sec, s) for sec, sents in SECTIONS.items() for s in sents]
tokens = lambda text: len(text.split())

query = set("opened pack spoiled photo".split())
score = lambda s: len(query & set(s.lower().replace(".", "").split()))
top = sorted(children, key=lambda c: -score(c[1]))[:3]

print("top 3 children (precise matches):")
for sec, s in top:
    print(f"  [{sec}] {s}")
child_text = " ".join(s for _, s in top)

parents = []                                        # replace each child by its parent, keeping order, without repeats
for sec, _ in top:
    if sec not in parents:
        parents.append(sec)
parent_text = " ".join(" ".join(SECTIONS[p]) for p in parents)
naive_text = " ".join(" ".join(SECTIONS[sec]) for sec, _ in top)

print(f"\nchildren only          {tokens(child_text):>3} words   mentions the 24-hour limit: {'24 hours' in child_text}")
print(f"parents, de-duplicated {tokens(parent_text):>3} words   mentions the 24-hour limit: {'24 hours' in parent_text}   ({len(parents)} sections)")
print(f"parents, not de-duped  {tokens(naive_text):>3} words   {len(top) - len(parents)} section sent twice")
blocks.caption: Children only, parents de-duplicated, and parents without de-duplication

blocks.text: The three best-matching sentences never mention the 24-hour limit, which is the first thing a customer with spoiled milk needs. Their parent section does. Returning parents without removing repeats sends the same section twice and pays for it twice.
How much can you trust the number?
A recall figure from a small golden set is an estimate with a wide margin. This computes the margin.

blocks.code:
# How far can you trust a recall number from a small golden set? Wilson 95% interval for a proportion.
import math


def wilson(hits, n, z=1.96):
    p = hits / n
    centre = (p + z * z / (2 * n)) / (1 + z * z / n)
    half = z * math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z * z / (4 * n * n)) / (1 + z * z / n)
    return centre - half, centre + half


print("measured recall of 80% on golden sets of different sizes")
for n in (10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500):
    lo, hi = wilson(round(0.8 * n), n)
    print(f"  {n:>3} questions: the true value is plausibly between {lo:.0%} and {hi:.0%}  (width {hi - lo:.0%})")

print("\ndid the change help? before 32/40 = 80%, after 35/40 = 88%")
(lo1, hi1), (lo2, hi2) = wilson(32, 40), wilson(35, 40)
print(f"  before {lo1:.0%}-{hi1:.0%}, after {lo2:.0%}-{hi2:.0%}: the ranges overlap heavily, so 3 more questions is not evidence yet")
print("  look at which questions flipped: 3 fixed and 0 broken is a stronger signal than the two totals")
blocks.caption: The plausible range around a measured 80%, at six golden-set sizes

blocks.text: With 20 questions, a measured 80% is compatible with anything from 58% to 92%. A change that moves recall from 80% to 88% on 40 questions is three questions, and the two ranges overlap heavily. Two habits follow. Grow the set towards a hundred or more questions for decisions that matter. And compare per question, not per total: three questions fixed and none broken tells you more than two percentages.
Which metric answers which question

rows: Did we retrieve the passage at all?
Is the first good result near the top?
Are the best results ordered best-first?
How much of what we sent was noise?
Is the answer supported by what we sent?
Does the answer address the question?

blocks.text: Report retrieval metrics at the k you actually use: the k passed to the reranker, and the smaller k passed to the model.
What people get wrong about this module

items: "GraphRAG is the advanced version, so it is better." It answers a different kind of question. On single-passage lookups it adds cost and new ways to be wrong.
"Agentic RAG replaces the pipeline." It replaces one retrieval with a loop of several model calls. Use it for the questions the pipeline measurably fails.
"HyDE improves retrieval." Sometimes. When the model's guess is far from your domain it pulls the search the wrong way.
"We added citations, so answers are grounded." A citation is a claim of support. Check that the quote exists in the cited chunk.
"Recall@20 is 95%, retrieval is done." If five chunks reach the model, recall@5 and the ordering are what count.
"The score went up, ship it." On forty questions, a few points is noise. Look at which questions changed.

blocks.text: Practice: five problems

blocks.title: A question has 4 relevant chunks. Your retriever's top 5 contains 3 of them, at ranks 2, 3 and 5. What are recall@5, recall@3 and the reciprocal rank?
blocks.text: Recall@5 = 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75. Recall@3 = 2 ÷ 4 = 0.50, since only ranks 2 and 3 fall inside the top 3. The reciprocal rank is 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5, because the first relevant result is at rank 2.

blocks.title: The top 5 results have relevance grades 0, 2, 1, 0, 0, and those are the only two relevant chunks. Compute nDCG@5.
blocks.text: DCG = 2 ÷ log₂(3) + 1 ÷ log₂(4) = 1.262 + 0.5 = 1.762. The ideal order is 2, 1: IDCG = 2 ÷ log₂(2) + 1 ÷ log₂(3) = 2 + 0.631 = 2.631. nDCG = 1.762 ÷ 2.631 = 0.67. Moving both up one rank would make it 1.0.

blocks.title: You apply contextual retrieval to a document of 8,000 tokens split into 40 chunks of 200 tokens. How many input tokens are processed without prompt caching, and what is the full-price equivalent with caching at one tenth for cached reads?
blocks.text: Without caching every call sends the document and a chunk: 40 × 8,200 = 328,000. With caching the first call pays 8,200 in full; the other 39 pay 800 for the cached document plus 200 for the chunk: 39 × 1,000 = 39,000. Total 47,200, about seven times less. The cache-write premium on the first call adds a little.

blocks.title: Your golden set has 25 questions and recall@5 rose from 76% to 84% after you added a reranker. Should you conclude the reranker helps?
blocks.text: That is 19 correct becoming 21: two questions. With 25 questions the margin on either figure is roughly ±16 points, so the totals cannot settle it. Check the per-question changes, confirm that nDCG rose (a reranker should improve ordering, not candidate recall), and grow the set before making the decision permanent.

blocks.title: Retrieval is good on first questions and poor on follow-ups, and you have a 150 ms budget before the search. What do you add, and how do you keep it inside the budget?
blocks.text: Rewrite the latest turn into a standalone question using the conversation, with a small fast model and a short output. Skip the rewrite on the first turn, and skip it when the message already names its subject. Run it in parallel with anything that does not depend on it, and fall back to the raw message if it has not returned in time.
Your golden set and ablation log
The build step asks for a 40-question golden set and before-and-after numbers. Keep two files in the repository.

headers: Golden set: one row per question
rows: Question as a user would type it
Standalone form, if it is a follow-up
so retrieval can be tested with and without rewriting
Ids of the chunks that answer it, with grades
Why this question is in the set

blocks.text: The ablation log is one line per experiment: date, the single thing changed, recall@k, MRR, nDCG, latency added, questions fixed, questions broken, and the decision. It is the difference between a retriever you understand and one that happens to work this week.

lessons.title: Advanced RAG and measuring retrieval: build and practise

blocks.text: Add heading-aware parsing, contextual chunk headers, query rewriting for follow-up questions, and sentence-level citations to the assistant. Build a 40-question golden set and report recall@5, MRR and nDCG before and after each change.
Recall@k, MRR and nDCG computed by hand on a labelled set

blocks.code:
# Recall@k, MRR and nDCG on a tiny labelled set. relevant = {chunk_id: grade}, grade 2 = best.
import math

runs = [
    {"q": "refund window for dairy",  "relevant": {"c7": 2, "c9": 1}, "retrieved": ["c2", "c7", "c9", "c4", "c1"]},
    {"q": "change delivery slot",     "relevant": {"c3": 2},          "retrieved": ["c3", "c8", "c5", "c6", "c2"]},
    {"q": "damaged item replacement", "relevant": {"c5": 2, "c1": 1}, "retrieved": ["c4", "c6", "c8", "c2", "c5"]},
    {"q": "cash on delivery limit",   "relevant": {"c11": 2},         "retrieved": ["c1", "c2", "c3", "c4", "c5"]},
]


def recall_at_k(run, k):
    found = [c for c in run["retrieved"][:k] if c in run["relevant"]]
    return len(found) / len(run["relevant"])


def reciprocal_rank(run):
    for rank, c in enumerate(run["retrieved"], start=1):
        if c in run["relevant"]:
            return 1 / rank
    return 0.0


def ndcg_at_k(run, k):
    dcg = sum(run["relevant"].get(c, 0) / math.log2(rank + 1) for rank, c in enumerate(run["retrieved"][:k], start=1))
    ideal = sorted(run["relevant"].values(), reverse=True)[:k]
    idcg = sum(g / math.log2(rank + 1) for rank, g in enumerate(ideal, start=1))
    return dcg / idcg


print(f"{'question':26} recall@3  recall@5  RR    nDCG@5")
for r in runs:
    print(f"{r['q']:26} {recall_at_k(r, 3):<9.2f} {recall_at_k(r, 5):<9.2f} {reciprocal_rank(r):<5.2f} {ndcg_at_k(r, 5):.2f}")
n = len(runs)
print(f"{'MEAN':26} {sum(recall_at_k(r, 3) for r in runs) / n:<9.2f} {sum(recall_at_k(r, 5) for r in runs) / n:<9.2f} "
      f"{sum(reciprocal_rank(r) for r in runs) / n:<5.2f} {sum(ndcg_at_k(r, 5) for r in runs) / n:.2f}")
blocks.caption: retrieval_metrics.py

blocks.title: Recall@20 is 92% but users say answers are often wrong. Walk through your investigation.
blocks.text: High recall@20 says the passage is usually retrieved somewhere in 20. Check recall@k at the k actually sent to the model, and nDCG: the passage may sit at rank 14. Add or fix reranking. Then check faithfulness on cases where the passage was in context; if those fail, look at chunk quality (broken tables), context size, and the answer prompt.

blocks.title: How would you keep a RAG index correct as documents are edited and deleted daily?
blocks.text: Give every document a stable id and content hash. On change, re-parse, diff or replace that document's chunks in one transaction, and delete chunks of removed documents. Store source version and timestamp on each chunk, filter out superseded versions at query time, and run a nightly reconciliation that compares the source list with the index.

modules.title: M6 · Agents: the loop and its controls
modules.summary: The journey built one authorised agent. Here you learn every moving part of the loop, and above all how to make it stop, remember and ask.

blocks.text: You describe functions to the model as a name, a description and a JSON schema. The model does not run anything: it outputs a request to call a tool with arguments, your code runs it and sends the result back.
How it behaves

The description is a prompt. Say what the tool does, when to use it and when not to, and what it returns. Few well-designed tools beat many thin ones; return compact, meaningful results and helpful error messages the model can act on. Models can request several tools in one turn, which you can run in parallel. Tool definitions are tokens in every request.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Thirty near-duplicate tools with one-line descriptions. The model picks the wrong one and each definition is paid for on every call.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: tools (name, description, schema) → model emits tool call + args → your code validates and runs → tool result → model continues

blocks.title: The model keeps choosing the wrong tool between search_orders and get_order. How do you fix it?
blocks.text: Improve the definitions: state clearly when each applies, what inputs it needs, and how they differ, or merge them into one tool with an optional parameter. Then add those cases to a tool-selection eval.
An agent is a model calling tools in a loop until the task is done. Each turn: send the conversation, get back either a final answer or tool calls, run the tools, append results, repeat.
How it behaves

Your code owns the loop. That is where you put limits, logging, approval gates and error handling. The loop ends when the model stops asking for tools or one of your limits fires. Every iteration resends the whole growing context, so cost grows faster than the step count.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Treating the framework's loop as a black box. When it misbehaves you cannot see or change the part that matters.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: messages → model → tool calls? → yes: run tools, append results, loop → no: final answer

blocks.title: Write the agent loop in words, including where safety controls go.
blocks.text: While under the step and budget limits: call the model with messages and tools; if it returns tool calls, validate each, check permissions and approval rules, execute, append results, continue; if it returns text only, return it. Limits, authorisation and logging all sit in your loop code.
ReAct (reason + act) interleaves a short thought, an action and the observation that comes back, repeated. The thought states what the model will do and why before it does it.
How it behaves

It was introduced as a prompting pattern with text parsing. Native tool calling plus reasoning models now implement the same cycle without a "Thought:/Action:" text format, but the cycle itself is still how every agent works. Visible reasoning between steps is useful for debugging traces.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Building a regex parser for "Action: search[...]" text today instead of using the provider's tool-calling API.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: thought → action (tool call) → observation (result) → thought → … → final answer

blocks.title: What is ReAct and is it still relevant with native tool calling?
blocks.text: It is the reason-act-observe cycle. The original text format is obsolete, but the pattern is exactly what a tool-calling loop does. Knowing it explains why agents can recover from a failed step: the observation feeds the next reasoning.
Planning means the agent lays out the steps before acting. A written plan keeps a long task on track and gives a human something to review before work starts.
How it behaves

Variants: plan-then-execute (one planning call, then steps, replan on failure), and a living to-do list the agent updates as it goes. A plan stored outside the context survives compaction. Planning helps on long multi-step tasks and hurts on short ones by adding a call. Good agents replan when observations contradict the plan.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Executing a ten-step plan to the end after step two showed the assumption was wrong.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: goal → draft plan (steps) → human or code approves → execute step → result matches plan? → no: replan → yes: next step

blocks.title: When is plan-then-execute better than a plain reactive loop?
blocks.text: For long tasks with many dependent steps, when a human should approve the approach first, or when steps can be run in parallel once known. A reactive loop is better for short or exploratory tasks.
Reflection is a pass where the output is critiqued and then revised. The critic can be the same model with a review prompt, a different model, or code such as tests and linters.
How it behaves

Grounded feedback is what makes it work: a failing test, a schema error, a rule checklist, a fresh reviewer that did not see the reasoning. A model re-reading its own answer with no new information tends to approve it. Cap the rounds, since each is another full call.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: "Review your answer and improve it" with no criteria. It costs a call and mostly rephrases.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: draft → evaluator (tests, rules, separate reviewer) → pass? → yes: done → no: feedback → revise → re-evaluate (max N rounds)

blocks.title: Why is self-critique often ineffective and what makes reflection work?
blocks.text: The same model with the same context shares the blind spots that produced the error. It works when the critique brings new information: executed tests, validation errors, explicit rubrics, or an independent reviewer with fresh context.
A stop condition is any rule that ends the loop. Without them an agent can run forever, spend unbounded money, or repeat the same failing call.
How it behaves

Use several at once: the model finishes, maximum steps, token or money budget, wall-clock deadline, repeated identical tool call, repeated errors, and a "needs human" outcome. When a limit fires, return what was accomplished and why it stopped; do not pretend success.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Only relying on the model deciding it is done. A confused agent never decides that.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: each step → done? → steps over limit? → budget spent? → deadline passed? → same call repeated? → any yes: stop with reason

blocks.title: Name five stop conditions for a production agent.
blocks.text: The model returns a final answer; a maximum step count; a token or cost budget; a wall-clock timeout; loop detection on repeated identical tool calls or repeated errors. A sixth is escalation to a human.
Short-term memory is the conversation so far in the context window: messages, tool calls and results of the current task. The model has nothing else; your code resends it every turn.
How it behaves

It is bounded by the context window and degrades before the limit. Manage it: trim or summarise old turns, clear stale tool results, and keep a scratchpad of key facts. What you keep in it is the main lever on both quality and cost.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Keeping every raw tool result forever. By step 15 the context is mostly old JSON.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: turn → append messages + tool results → over budget? → trim or summarise oldest → send

blocks.title: What is an agent's short-term memory physically?
blocks.text: The list of messages your application sends with each request. The model is stateless, so anything not in that list, or not retrievable by a tool, does not exist for it.
Long-term memory is information stored outside the context that survives across sessions: user preferences, past decisions, learned facts. It is brought back by retrieval or by reading files.
How it behaves

Kinds: semantic (facts about the user or domain), episodic (what happened in earlier tasks), procedural (how to do things, i.e. instructions and skills). Stores range from a notes file the agent reads and edits, to a database, to a vector index. The hard parts are deciding what to write, keeping it current, and scoping it per user. Stored memory is untrusted input when read back.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Saving everything. Retrieval then returns stale and contradictory "memories" and the agent gets worse.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: session ends → extract durable facts → write to store (per user) → next session: retrieve relevant → inject into context

blocks.title: How would you give a shopping assistant memory of "no onion, no garlic"?
blocks.text: Extract it as a durable preference when stated, store it in a per-user profile record with a timestamp, and load the profile into the context at session start. Let the user view and delete it, and treat it as data, not instructions.

State is everything needed to continue a run: messages, plan, intermediate results, pending approvals. A checkpoint saves that state after each step so the run can pause, resume, retry or be replayed.
How it behaves

Durable state turns an agent from a single long function call into a resumable workflow. It enables human approval that arrives hours later, crash recovery without repaying for finished steps, and "time travel" debugging from any step. Tools with side effects must be idempotent, because a resumed step may run again.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Holding state only in process memory. A deploy mid-run loses a 20-step task.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: step → update state → save checkpoint (thread id) → crash or pause → load latest checkpoint → resume next step

blocks.title: Why do long-running agents need checkpoints?
blocks.text: So work survives crashes and deploys, so a human can approve later without a held connection, and so a failed run can resume from the last good step instead of restarting. It also gives a replayable record for debugging.
Human in the loop pauses the agent at defined points so a person can approve, edit or reject before it continues.
How it behaves

Gate by risk, not by default: reads run freely, reversible writes may run, irreversible or costly actions wait for approval. Show the person the exact action and arguments, not the model's summary of them. With checkpoints the run can wait for hours. Too many prompts cause approval fatigue, where people click yes without reading.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Asking for approval on every step. Within a day nobody reads the prompts.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: proposed action → risk tier? → low: run → high: pause, show exact action → approve / edit / reject → resume

blocks.title: Which agent actions should require human approval?
blocks.text: Those that are irreversible, cost money, affect other people, or leave the system: refunds, orders, deletes, sending messages, changing permissions. Read-only and easily undone actions should not, to avoid approval fatigue.

lessons.title: Go deeper: one task, every turn of the loop

A customer writes "the milk in order A17 was spoiled, please refund it". Here is the whole run, one row per trip around the loop. Read the middle column: on every model call the entire list so far is sent again.

blocks.text: Four model calls, three tool executions, one pause. The model chose the order of steps. Your code decided what was allowed, what needed a person, and when to stop. That division is the whole design.
What the message list looks like

Providers differ in field names, but every tool-calling API has this shape. A tool call and its result are linked by an id, and the result is sent back by you as the next message. This listing is abbreviated: it leaves out the policy search and the approval pause.

                                        "arguments": {"order_id": "A17"}}]},

                        "content": {"item": "milk 1L", "price": 68, "delivered": "today 09:10"}},

                        "content": {"refund_id": "R-881", "status": "approved"}},

]

blocks.text: Notice what is absent. There is no user id in any argument: your code adds it from the session. And a tool error would go in the same place as a result, as text the model can read and react to.
A tool definition is a prompt
The model chooses tools from their names and descriptions alone. Compare two definitions of the same tool.

Say when to use it and when not to

Describe what comes back, and what an error means
so the model's next step is sensible
