blocks.text: Checkpoints: what a crash costs
A long run will be interrupted: a deploy, a timeout, a wait for approval. This example kills the process after the refund step and restarts it, with and without checkpoints.

blocks.caption: The same crash, replayed from the start and resumed from a checkpoint

blocks.text: Without checkpoints the restart re-ran all four tools, seven executions for a four-step task, and the refund tool was called a second time. The customer was refunded once only because the tool took an idempotency key. Checkpoints save the repeated work; they do not replace idempotency, because a crash can land between a tool finishing and its checkpoint being written. Try that case in the lab.
Memory: a budget and a store
Short-term memory is the message list, and it must be trimmed. Long-term memory is a store, and it must be scoped per user, dated, and overwritten when facts change.

blocks.code:
# Short-term memory is a budget you trim. Long-term memory is a store you scope, date and overwrite.
def trim(messages, budget):
    """Keep pinned messages, then as many of the most recent as fit."""
    pinned = [m for m in messages if m.get("pin")]
    used = sum(m["tokens"] for m in pinned)
    kept = []
    for m in reversed([m for m in messages if not m.get("pin")]):
        if used + m["tokens"] > budget:
            break
        kept.append(m); used += m["tokens"]
    dropped = len(messages) - len(pinned) - len(kept)
    return pinned + kept[::-1], used, dropped


history = [{"role": "system", "tokens": 900, "pin": True, "text": "rules"},
           {"role": "user", "tokens": 60, "pin": True, "text": "never substitute brands"},
           *[{"role": "tool", "tokens": 700, "text": f"search result {i}"} for i in range(1, 9)],
           {"role": "user", "tokens": 40, "text": "add oat milk"}]
kept, used, dropped = trim(history, budget=3000)
print(f"short-term: {len(history)} messages, {sum(m['tokens'] for m in history)} tokens -> kept {len(kept)} ({used} tokens), dropped {dropped} old tool results")
print("            the early constraint survived because it is pinned:", any(m["text"] == "never substitute brands" for m in kept))

memory = []                                             # long-term: (user, key, value, day, days it stays valid)


def remember(user, key, value, day, valid_for=None):
    memory[:] = [m for m in memory if not (m[0] == user and m[1] == key)]      # newer fact replaces the older one
    memory.append((user, key, value, day, valid_for))


def recall(user, today):
    return {k: v for u, k, v, d, ttl in memory if u == user and (ttl is None or today - d <= ttl)}


remember("asha", "diet", "no onion, no garlic", day=10)                # a standing preference: no expiry
remember("asha", "milk", "cow milk", day=12)
remember("ravi", "diet", "vegan", day=15)
remember("asha", "milk", "oat milk", day=140)                          # she changed her mind
remember("asha", "gate_code", "4471 this week", day=150, valid_for=7)  # a temporary fact
print("\nlong-term, loaded for asha on day 200:", recall("asha", today=200))
print("            ravi's facts are never returned for asha; the gate code expired; milk shows the newer value")
blocks.caption: Trimming to a token budget with pinned messages, then a per-user fact store

items: Six old tool results were dropped and the customer's early instruction survived, because it was pinned. Unpinned, it would have been the first thing lost.
The long-term store returns only this user's facts, gives the newer milk preference, and lets a temporary fact expire while a standing preference does not.
What it does not do is decide what is worth remembering. That is a judgment call you make in the write path: standing preferences and decisions, yes; one-off details, no.

blocks.text: Approval that cannot be talked around
An approval step is a security control, so it has to hold when the model has been manipulated.

blocks.code:
# Human approval that cannot be talked around: tier by impact, show the real call, bind approval to that exact call.
import hashlib, json

TIER = {"get_order": "read", "search_policy": "read", "update_delivery_note": "reversible",
        "issue_refund": "approve", "cancel_order": "approve", "send_sms": "approve"}
approvals = {}                                          # fingerprint of an exact call -> who approved it

fingerprint = lambda call: hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(call, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()[:10]


def render(call):                                       # built by code from the structured call, never by the model
    return f"{call['tool']}(" + ", ".join(f"{k}={v!r}" for k, v in call["args"].items()) + ")"


def gate(call, model_summary=""):
    tier = TIER.get(call["tool"], "approve")            # unknown tools default to the strictest tier
    if tier in ("read", "reversible"):
        return f"RUN    {render(call)}   [{tier}]"
    fp = fingerprint(call)
    if fp in approvals:
        return f"RUN    {render(call)}   [approved by {approvals[fp]}]"
    shown = f"reviewer sees: {render(call)}"
    if model_summary:
        shown += f"   (model's own description ignored: {model_summary!r})"
    return f"PAUSE  {shown}"


refund = {"tool": "issue_refund", "args": {"order_id": "A17", "amount": 68}}
print(gate({"tool": "get_order", "args": {"order_id": "A17"}}))
print(gate({"tool": "update_delivery_note", "args": {"order_id": "A17", "note": "ring twice"}}))
print(gate(refund))
approvals[fingerprint(refund)] = "support_desk_4"
print(gate(refund))
print(gate({"tool": "issue_refund", "args": {"order_id": "A17", "amount": 6800}}))          # same tool, different amount
print(gate({"tool": "send_sms", "args": {"to": "+91-98xxxxxx01", "text": "all order history"}}, model_summary="send the customer a receipt"))
print(gate({"tool": "export_customers", "args": {}}))                                       # not in the table at all
blocks.caption: Tiers by impact, the real call shown to the reviewer, approval bound to that exact call

items: The approved refund of 68 ran. The same tool with 6,800 paused again: approval is for one exact call, identified by a fingerprint of its arguments.
The reviewer saw the real `send_sms` arguments, not the model's description of them. A manipulated model can describe anything.
A tool missing from the tier table paused by default. New tools start at the strictest tier.

blocks.text: Reflection that works and reflection that does not

rows: Failing test, compiler or linter output
A rule checklist applied point by point
A separate reviewer with fresh context
The environment's real state after the action
agents: did the refund actually exist?

blocks.text: What people get wrong about this module

items: "An agent is a smarter model." It is the same model inside a loop your code runs.
"The framework handles stopping." Read which limits it sets by default. Often the answer is a step count and nothing else.
"Checkpoints make retries safe." They reduce repeated work. Only idempotent tools make repeats harmless.
"The agent remembers the user." Only what you stored, scoped and loaded back.
"Approval prompts make it safe." Only if the reviewer sees the real call, and is not asked so often that they stop reading.
"More tools make it more capable." Past a handful, selection accuracy falls and every call costs more.

blocks.text: Practice: five problems

blocks.title: A four-step task crashes after step 3 has run. How many tool executions happen in total with no checkpoints, and how many with a checkpoint after every step?
blocks.text: Without checkpoints the restart begins again: 3 + 4 = 7 executions, with steps 1 to 3 run twice. With checkpoints it resumes at step 4: 3 + 1 = 4. If step 3 moved money, the first case needs an idempotency key to avoid doing it twice.

blocks.title: An agent has made the calls search("refund policy"), search("refunds policy"), search("policy on refunds"), search("refund policy"). Which of your stop conditions should fire, and what should the run return?
blocks.text: An exact-repeat detector fires on the fourth call, which matches the first. A near-duplicate detector or a cap on calls to one tool would have fired earlier. Return what was found, state that the search did not converge, and offer the fallback such as a human; do not present a guess as an answer.

blocks.title: Sort these tools into run freely, run but log, and needs approval: get_order, add_to_cart, update_delivery_note, issue_refund, send_sms, delete_account. Give the rule you used.
blocks.text: Run freely: get_order (read only). Run but log: add_to_cart and update_delivery_note (the customer can undo them). Needs approval: issue_refund (moves money), send_sms (leaves the system and reaches a person), delete_account (cannot be undone). The rule is impact: irreversible, costs money, or affects someone outside the conversation.

blocks.title: A conversation holds a 900-token system prompt, a 60-token user constraint from turn 1, and eight 700-token tool results, with a 3,000-token budget for history. What should be kept, and what is the risk if you simply keep the most recent messages?
blocks.text: Pin the system prompt and the constraint (960 tokens), then keep the newest tool results that fit: two of them, 1,400 tokens, for 2,360. Keeping only the most recent messages would drop the turn-1 constraint, and the agent would violate an instruction the customer gave at the start.

blocks.title: What exactly goes into a checkpoint so that a paused run can resume tomorrow on a different server?
blocks.text: The full message list including tool calls and results, the index of the next step, any plan or to-do list, pending approval requests with the exact call awaiting a decision, the run's budgets used so far (steps, tokens, time), the user and tenant, and the prompt and model versions. It is stored under a run id in a database, not in process memory.
Your agent specification
The build step rebuilds the order-status agent as a loop you own. Write this sheet first.

rows: name, when to use, arguments, what it returns, impact tier
which values are injected from the session, never taken from the model
maximum steps, token and cost budget, time limit, repeat detection, the "escalate to a human" outcome
which tiers pause, who approves, what the reviewer is shown, how long a request stays valid
what a checkpoint contains, where it is stored, how a run resumes
the key for every write tool
what is pinned, the history budget, which facts are written to long-term memory and their lifetime
what the user sees for each stop reason

blocks.text: Rebuild the order-status agent as an explicit loop you own: tool schemas, step limit, token budget, checkpoint after each step, and a human approval gate before any refund.
An agent loop with four stop conditions, driven by a scripted fake model

blocks.caption: agent_loop.py

blocks.title: An agent called the same search tool 40 times with slightly different queries and never answered. What controls were missing?
blocks.text: A maximum step count, a token or cost budget, loop detection for repeated near-identical calls, and an instruction plus an allowed outcome for "I could not find this". Also check the tool's results: empty or unhelpful output gives the model nothing to converge on.

blocks.title: Design a refund agent for the grocery app that is safe to put in production.
blocks.text: Tools: read order (user id from session), check policy (retrieval), propose refund. The refund tool takes an idempotency key, enforces amount limits in code, and above a threshold pauses for human approval showing exact order and amount. Loop has step, budget and time limits, checkpoints each step, logs every tool call, and returns "escalated to support" as a valid outcome. Evaluated on trajectories including injected instructions inside order notes.

modules.title: M7 · Agent ecosystems: protocols, context and teams
modules.summary: Protocols that let agents plug into tools and each other, the craft of deciding what goes in the context, and the frameworks you will be asked about.

blocks.text: The Model Context Protocol is an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data. An MCP server exposes three kinds of things: tools (functions the model can call), resources (data to read) and prompts (reusable templates).
How it behaves

A server runs locally over stdio or remotely over streamable HTTP with OAuth. Write the server once and any MCP-capable client can use it, instead of one integration per app. Designing one is designing an API for a model: few tools shaped around tasks, clear descriptions, small results, useful errors.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Wrapping all 80 endpoints of a REST API as 80 tools. Shape tools around what a user wants done.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: your API or data → MCP server (tools, resources, prompts) → stdio or HTTP + OAuth → any MCP client

blocks.title: What does an MCP server expose and how is that different from plain tool calling?
blocks.text: Tools, resources and prompts over a standard protocol. Tool calling is the model-side mechanism; MCP standardises how those tools are discovered and invoked across applications, so one server serves many clients.
The MCP client lives inside the host application (an IDE, a chat app, your agent). It connects to servers, lists their tools, and passes tool calls and results between the model and the server.
How it behaves

The host decides which servers to trust, which tools to show the model, and what needs user approval. Every connected server's tool definitions cost context tokens, so mature hosts load tools on demand or search them rather than injecting everything. The client must treat tool descriptions and results as untrusted.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Connecting fifteen servers and wondering why the agent is slow, expensive and picks odd tools.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: host app → MCP client → connect + list tools → give selected tools to model → model calls → client forwards → result back

blocks.title: What are the roles of host, client and server in MCP?
blocks.text: The host is the application the user runs. The client is the connector inside it that speaks the protocol to one server. The server provides tools, resources and prompts. The host owns trust and approval decisions.

A skill is a folder containing instructions (a `SKILL.md` with a name and description) plus optional scripts and reference files. The agent sees only the short description until a task matches, then loads the full instructions.
How it behaves

This is progressive disclosure: hundreds of skills cost a line each until used. Skills carry procedural knowledge (how your team does a release, how to fill a form) rather than connectivity. They pair with MCP: MCP gives access to systems, skills tell the agent how to use them well.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Pasting every procedure into the system prompt, paying for all of them on every request.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: skill descriptions in context (one line each) → task matches → load SKILL.md → read extra files or run scripts as needed

blocks.title: How do skills differ from MCP tools?
blocks.text: MCP tools give the agent capabilities: functions that reach external systems. Skills give it know-how: instructions and scripts loaded on demand. One connects, the other teaches procedure.

Context engineering is deciding what occupies the context window at each step: instructions, tools, retrieved knowledge, memory, history. It is the successor to prompt engineering for systems that run many turns.
How it behaves

The working principle is the smallest set of high-signal tokens that makes the right behaviour likely. Tactics: retrieve just in time instead of preloading, keep tool results compact, write notes to files, isolate side work in sub-agents that return a summary, and order content stable-first for caching. More context is not better; irrelevant context lowers accuracy.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Preloading every document "in case it is useful", which makes the model slower, costlier and less accurate.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: task → select (what is needed now) → compress (trim, summarise) → isolate (sub-agent for side work) → write (notes outside context) → model call

blocks.title: What is context engineering and how is it different from prompt engineering?
blocks.text: Prompt engineering writes one good instruction. Context engineering manages everything the model sees across a long run: which tools, which retrieved facts, which history, in what order, and what is kept outside the window. The goal is high signal per token.
When the conversation nears the context limit, compaction replaces older turns with a summary and continues from there.
How it behaves

A good summary keeps the goal, decisions made, current state, open problems and exact identifiers such as file paths and ids; it drops raw tool output and dead ends. Lighter options run first: clearing old tool results, or trimming. Compaction is lossy, so keep critical state (plan, to-do list, key facts) in files or structured state the agent can re-read afterwards.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Summarising so aggressively that the agent forgets a constraint the user gave at the start and violates it.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: context near limit → clear old tool results → still high? summarise older turns (keep goal, decisions, ids) → continue with summary + recent turns

blocks.title: What must a compaction summary preserve?
blocks.text: The user's goal and constraints, decisions and their reasons, the current state of the work, unresolved issues, and precise identifiers needed to continue. It can drop verbose tool output and abandoned attempts.
A handoff transfers control of the conversation from one agent to another that has different instructions and tools, such as a triage agent passing a billing question to a billing agent.
How it behaves

The receiving agent only knows what is handed to it, so the handoff message must carry the goal, relevant facts and what has been tried. Handoffs suit distinct domains with separate tools and permissions. Each hop risks losing context and adds latency.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Handing off with "user needs help with billing" and losing the order id the user already gave.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: triage agent → decide specialist → handoff with goal + facts + history summary → specialist continues with own tools

blocks.title: What information must accompany a handoff between agents?
blocks.text: The user's goal, the facts already collected (ids, constraints), what was attempted and the result, and what the receiving agent is expected to produce. Otherwise the user is asked the same questions again.
A lead agent breaks a task into parts, gives each to a worker sub-agent with a fresh context, and combines the summaries they return.
How it behaves

Benefits: parallel work, and each worker spends its own context on exploration while the lead's context stays clean. Costs: several times the tokens, and coordination errors when the brief is vague. It pays off for broad, parallelisable work such as research across many sources, and loses on tightly coupled work where every part needs the same shared context.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Splitting a small coupled coding task across five agents that then make incompatible assumptions.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: lead plans subtasks → spawn workers in parallel (own context, clear brief) → each returns a summary → lead synthesises

blocks.title: When does a multi-agent design beat a single agent, and what does it cost?
blocks.text: When the task splits into independent parts that can run in parallel and would overflow one context. It costs several times more tokens and adds coordination risk, so use it for breadth-first work, not for tightly dependent steps.
LangGraph is a library for building agents as a graph: nodes are functions or model calls, edges (including conditional ones) decide what runs next, and a shared typed state flows through.
How it behaves

Its value is control and durability: explicit cycles, checkpointing of state per thread, interrupts for human approval, streaming, and replay from any checkpoint. You trade some simplicity for a structure you can see, test and resume. LangChain is the older, broader toolkit of model and retriever wrappers from the same team; LangGraph is its orchestration layer.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Reaching for a graph framework for a single prompt with one tool.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: define state → add nodes → add edges + conditional edges → compile with checkpointer → invoke with thread id → interrupt and resume

blocks.title: What does LangGraph give you that a hand-written loop does not?
blocks.text: Built-in persistence and checkpoints, interrupt and resume for human approval, a visible graph of control flow, and replay for debugging. A hand-written loop is simpler and fine until you need those.

A lightweight framework with a small set of primitives: agents (instructions plus tools), handoffs between agents, guardrails that validate input and output, and sessions for history, with tracing built in.
How it behaves

It runs the tool loop for you and makes handoff-style multi-agent systems short to write. Most providers now ship an equivalent agent SDK, and CrewAI covers similar ground with role-based "crews". AutoGen, an early conversation-based framework, is now archived, and its repository points new users to Microsoft Agent Framework. The concepts carry over between all of them: loop, tools, handoffs, guardrails, state, tracing.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Learning a framework's API before understanding the loop it hides. Frameworks change yearly; the loop does not.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: define agents + tools → runner starts loop → tool calls and handoffs → guardrails check → final output + trace

blocks.title: You know one agent framework. How do you approach learning another?
blocks.text: Map its primitives to the common concepts: how it defines tools, runs the loop, passes control between agents, validates input and output, persists state, and traces. The differences are mostly naming and defaults.

Agent2Agent (A2A) is an open protocol for agents built by different teams or vendors to talk to each other. An agent publishes an Agent Card describing its skills and endpoint; a client agent sends it a task and receives status updates and results.
How it behaves

Where MCP connects an agent to tools, A2A connects an agent to another agent treated as an opaque peer with its own internal reasoning. Tasks are long-running with states, can stream, and carry authentication. It started at Google and is now an open-governance project with a published version 1.0. Adoption is still early, so treat it as something to recognise and evaluate rather than assume.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Confusing it with MCP. Use MCP to give your agent a tool; A2A to delegate a whole task to someone else's agent.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: discover Agent Card → send task → remote agent works (opaque) → status updates / stream → artifacts returned

blocks.title: MCP versus A2A in one sentence each.
blocks.text: MCP standardises how an agent uses tools and data sources. A2A standardises how one agent delegates tasks to and exchanges results with another independent agent.

lessons.title: Go deeper: four ways out of the context window

blocks.text: Go deeper: four ways out of the context window

An agent can only work with what is in its window. This module's ten topics are four different answers to "where does the rest live?" The protocol details below were checked against the published specifications on 12 November 2026: MCP revision 2026-07-28, the Agent Skills specification, and A2A version 1.0. They change; check the date before you rely on a field name.

headers: What stays out of the window until needed
rows: the system itself; only tool definitions and results come in
the instructions; only a one-line description is loaded up front
to explore without filling its own window
the exploration; only a summary comes back
to hand a whole job to someone else's agent
everything; only task status and results come back
to keep going past the limit
old turns; a summary and the files remain

blocks.text: MCP on the wire
Under the SDKs, MCP is JSON-RPC. Two messages carry almost everything an agent does with a server. This is a `tools/list` result for the grocery server, in the shape the specification defines:
A call, its normal result, and the two kinds of failure:

rows: Two standard transports: stdio for a local subprocess, Streamable HTTP for remote
local servers run with your user's permissions; remote ones need authorization
This revision has no connection handshake or session; every request carries its protocol version and client details
older tutorials describe an `initialize` step that newer servers no longer require
Servers should return tools in a deterministic order
a stable tool list keeps your prompt prefix cacheable
Tool execution errors come back as results with `isError: true`
pass them to the model so it can correct its call
Clients must treat tool annotations as untrusted unless the server is trusted
a server calling its own tool "read-only" proves nothing
State across calls is an explicit handle returned by one tool and passed to the next
design a `create_basket` that returns an id; do not rely on the connection
There should be a human able to deny tool invocations
approval belongs in the host, as in Module 6

blocks.text: The same two messages, running

This toy answers `tools/list` and `tools/call` in those shapes so you can see both error paths. It is not a conforming server: it omits the required request metadata, the transport and authorization. Build real servers with an official SDK.

blocks.caption: Discovery, a good call, a tool error the model can fix, and a protocol error it cannot

blocks.text: The middle line is the design point. "No order with that id. Ask the customer to check the id" is written for the model: it says what went wrong and what to do next. A bare "404" would leave the model guessing another id.
A skill on disk

A skill is a directory with a `SKILL.md`. The frontmatter is what the agent sees at startup; the body is loaded only when the description matches the task; other files are read only if the body points to them.

blocks.code:
returns-procedure/
├── SKILL.md              required: frontmatter + instructions
├── references/
│   └── edge-cases.md     read only when the instructions point here
└── scripts/
    └── refund_limit.py   run only when needed

---
name: returns-procedure
description: Handles a customer's return or refund request for a grocery
  order. Use when the customer reports a damaged, spoiled, missing or
  wrong item, or asks how to return something.
---
# Returns procedure
1. Look up the order with get_order. Never ask the customer for their user id.
2. Find the rule with search_policy for the item's category.
3. Dairy and frozen: reported within 24 hours, photo required.
4. Refunds above 500 rupees need a human approval.
See references/edge-cases.md for clearance items and partial refunds.

rows: at most 64 characters; lowercase letters, digits and hyphens; no leading, trailing or doubled hyphens; must match the directory name
at most 1,024 characters; say what the skill does and when to use it, with the words a user would use
name and description only, roughly 100 tokens per skill
the whole `SKILL.md` body; keep it under about 5,000 tokens and 500 lines

blocks.code:
# Progressive disclosure for skills: validate the frontmatter, then count what each loading strategy costs.
import re

SKILL_MD = """---
name: returns-procedure
description: Handles a customer's return or refund request for a grocery order. Use when the customer reports a damaged, spoiled, missing or wrong item, or asks how to return something.
---
# Returns procedure
1. Look up the order with get_order. Never ask the customer for their user id.
2. Find the rule with search_policy for the item's category.
3. Dairy and frozen: reported within 24 hours, photo required.
4. Refunds above 500 rupees need a human approval.
See references/edge-cases.md for clearance items and partial refunds.
"""


def parse(text):
    _, front, body = text.split("---\n", 2)
    meta = dict(line.split(": ", 1) for line in front.strip().split("\n"))
    return meta, body


def validate(meta, directory):
    problems = []
    name = meta.get("name", "")
    if not re.fullmatch(r"[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*", name) or len(name) > 64:
        problems.append("name: lowercase letters, digits and single hyphens, at most 64 characters")
    if name != directory:
        problems.append("name must match the directory name")
    if not 1 <= len(meta.get("description", "")) <= 1024:
        problems.append("description: 1 to 1024 characters")
    return problems or ["valid"]


meta, body = parse(SKILL_MD)
tok = lambda s: round(len(s) / 4)                       # rough: 4 characters per token
print("returns-procedure/SKILL.md ->", validate(meta, "returns-procedure"))
print("Returns_Procedure/SKILL.md ->", validate({**meta, "name": "Returns_Procedure"}, "Returns_Procedure"))
print(f"\nmetadata {tok(meta['name'] + meta['description'])} tokens, body {tok(body)} tokens")

N, META, BODY = 40, 100, 3000                           # 40 skills, typical sizes
print(f"\n{N} skills installed, one task that needs one of them")
print(f"  everything in the system prompt   {N * (META + BODY):>7,} tokens on every request")
print(f"  progressive disclosure            {N * META + BODY:>7,} tokens: {N} descriptions + the one body that matched")
blocks.caption: Validating the frontmatter, then the cost of loading everything versus loading on demand

blocks.text: The description is the trigger. "Helps with returns" would rarely be matched; the version above names the situations a customer actually describes.
Context engineering: four moves
Every technique in this module is one of four moves on the context window.

rows: bring in only what this step needs
retrieve just in time; load a skill on match; search tools instead of listing all
clear old tool results; summarise old turns; return compact tool output
do the messy work in another window
a sub-agent explores and returns a summary
keep it outside and read it back
a plan or notes file; long-term memory; a checkpoint

blocks.code:
# Context compaction in two stages: clear stale tool results first, summarise only if still too big.
LIMIT = 6000
messages = [
    {"kind": "system", "tokens": 900, "text": "rules"},
    {"kind": "user", "tokens": 80, "text": "Plan a week of dinners for 4. Constraint: no onion, no garlic. Budget 3,000 rupees."},
    *[{"kind": "tool_result", "tokens": 900, "text": f"search results page {i}", "step": i} for i in range(1, 9)],
    {"kind": "assistant", "tokens": 300, "text": "Decided: 5 vegetarian dinners, 2 with paneer. Basket id bsk_41."},
    {"kind": "tool_result", "tokens": 900, "text": "search results page 9", "step": 9},
    {"kind": "user", "tokens": 30, "text": "swap Tuesday for something quicker"},
]
total = lambda ms: sum(m["tokens"] for m in ms)
print(f"before          {total(messages):>6,} tokens in {len(messages)} messages   (limit {LIMIT:,})")

# Stage 1: replace all but the 2 most recent tool results with a one-line stub. Lossless for the plan.
recent = sorted(m["step"] for m in messages if m["kind"] == "tool_result")[-2:]
stage1 = [m if m["kind"] != "tool_result" or m["step"] in recent
          else {**m, "tokens": 15, "text": f"[result of step {m['step']} cleared; re-run the search if needed]"} for m in messages]
print(f"clear old tools {total(stage1):>6,} tokens   nothing the user said was touched")

# Stage 2 (only if still over): summarise everything except system, the latest user turn, and what must survive.
MUST_KEEP = ["no onion, no garlic", "3,000 rupees", "bsk_41"]
summary = {"kind": "summary", "tokens": 180,
           "text": "Goal: week of dinners for 4. Constraints: no onion, no garlic; budget 3,000 rupees. "
                   "Decided: 5 vegetarian, 2 paneer. Basket bsk_41. Open: Tuesday needs a quicker dish."}
stage2 = [messages[0], summary, messages[-1]]
print(f"if still over   {total(stage2):>6,} tokens in {len(stage2)} messages after summarising (not needed here: stage 1 was enough)")
for item in MUST_KEEP:
    print(f"  survives in the summary: {item!r:24} {item in summary['text']}")
bad = "Goal: week of dinners. Decided: 5 vegetarian, 2 paneer."
print(f"  a careless summary keeps the constraint: {'no onion' in bad}   <- this is how agents 'forget' instructions")
blocks.caption: Clearing stale tool results first, and what a summary must not lose

blocks.text: Clearing old tool results cut the context by two thirds and lost nothing the user said, so no summary was needed. Summarising is the lossy step; do it second, and state in the summary prompt what must survive: the goal, the constraints, the decisions, and exact identifiers. The last line shows the failure everyone eventually meets: a tidy summary that silently drops "no onion, no garlic".
One agent or several?

rows: Do the parts depend on each other's details?
no: they can run without talking
Would the work overflow one context?
yes: each part needs heavy exploration
Do parts need different tools or permissions?
yes: separate tools and credentials per agent
yes: parts can run in parallel

blocks.text: When you do split, the brief is the whole interface. A worker knows only what you put in it.

blocks.code:
Goal: find the cheapest in-stock substitute for each of these 6 items.
Context: the customer is vegetarian and has asked for no onion or garlic.
Already done: items 1-2 were matched by the customer; do not change them.
You may use: search_catalog, get_price. Do not modify the basket.
Return: a table of item, substitute, price, and one line on why.
  Say "none found" for an item rather than choosing a poor match.

blocks.text: A2A in one screen
A2A is for delegating to an agent you do not control and cannot see inside. From version 1.0 of the specification:

rows: a JSON description published at `/.well-known/agent-card.json`: name, description, supported interfaces, capabilities, skills, security schemes
submitted, working, input required, auth required, completed, failed, canceled, rejected
JSON-RPC, gRPC, and HTTP with JSON

blocks.text: Real cross-company use is still thin. Know the shape, be able to contrast it with MCP in an interview, and do not make a production design depend on it yet.
Frameworks: the same ideas under different names

This table maps concepts to the names each framework uses. It was checked against each framework's documentation on 12 November 2026; names still change between releases, so confirm them before relying on one. AutoGen is not in the table: its repository is archived and points new users to Microsoft Agent Framework.

rows: crew with a process (sequential or hierarchical)
task order, or a manager agent
tool approval that pauses the run
sessions for history; a serialised run state for paused runs

blocks.text: Learn one well. The second takes a weekend, because the loop underneath is the one from Module 6.
What people get wrong about this module

items: "MCP makes a tool safe." It makes a tool reachable. Trust, scopes and approval are still yours to design.
"Connect every server; the model will pick." Each tool definition is paid for on every call and makes the choice harder.
"Skills and MCP compete." One is know-how, the other is access. Most useful setups have both.
"Multi-agent is the advanced architecture." It is the expensive one. Many strong systems are one agent with good tools and context.
"A summary keeps what matters." Only if you said what matters. Constraints are the first thing lost.
"The framework is the hard part." The loop, the tools and the evals are. Frameworks change every year.

blocks.text: Practice: five problems

blocks.title: An agent is connected to 6 MCP servers with 12 tools each, and a tool definition averages 150 tokens. How many tokens of definitions go in every model call, and across a 20-step task? What two changes reduce it?
blocks.text: 6 × 12 × 150 = 10,800 tokens per call, and 216,000 across 20 steps. Caching makes most of that cheap but it still occupies the window and dilutes tool choice. Load a small core set and find the rest by tool search, and keep the tool list in a fixed order so the prefix stays cached.

blocks.title: You have 40 skills averaging 100 tokens of metadata and 3,000 tokens of instructions. Compare the context cost of putting them all in the system prompt with progressive disclosure, for a task that uses one skill.
blocks.text: All in the prompt: 40 × 3,100 = 124,000 tokens on every request. Progressive disclosure: 40 × 100 = 4,000 for the descriptions plus 3,000 for the one body, 7,000 in total. The saving is 94%, and the other 39 procedures are not there to distract the model.

blocks.title: A lead agent splits research into 4 parts. Each worker reads about 30,000 tokens and returns a 1,500-token summary. How much does the lead's context grow, compared with doing all the reading itself, and what is the catch?
blocks.text: The lead's context grows by 4 × 1,500 = 6,000 tokens instead of 120,000, so it stays sharp and under its limit. The catch is total cost and coordination: the system as a whole processes at least as many tokens, each worker pays its own overhead, and anything a worker left out of its summary is gone.

blocks.title: An MCP tool call fails in two different ways: the order id does not exist, and the tool name does not exist. How does each come back, and what should the client do with it?
blocks.text: A missing order is a tool execution error: a normal result with isError true and a message the model can act on, which the client passes to the model so it can ask for the right id. An unknown tool is a protocol error, a JSON-RPC error with a code such as -32602, which usually means the client or its tool list is wrong and should be logged and fixed.

blocks.title: Write the rule for what a compaction summary must preserve, and name the cheaper step you would try before summarising at all.
blocks.text: Preserve the user's goal and every constraint they gave, the decisions made and why, the current state of the work, open problems, and exact identifiers such as ids, paths and amounts. Before summarising, clear or shorten old tool results, which is nearly lossless. Keep the most important constraints pinned outside the summarised region so no summary can drop them.
Your MCP server design sheet
The build step exposes the grocery order tools as an MCP server. Decide these before choosing an SDK.

rows: 3 to 6, each named for a task; description says when to use it and what comes back
compact text plus `structuredContent` where a program will read it; a size cap and pagination
which failures are tool errors with guidance for the model, and which are protocol errors
how the caller is authenticated; that no tool accepts a user id as an argument
which tools create a handle, how long it lives, what an expired handle returns
stdio for local development, Streamable HTTP with authorization for anything shared
tools returned in a fixed order
Trust notes for users of the server
what each tool can change, and which should require confirmation

lessons.title: Agent ecosystems: protocols, context and teams: build and practise

blocks.text: Expose the grocery order tools as an MCP server, package the returns procedure as a skill, add context compaction to the loop, and try one orchestrator with two workers on a multi-order question.

blocks.title: Your agent has 60 MCP tools connected and quality has dropped. What do you change?
blocks.text: Reduce what is in context: keep a small core set always loaded and expose the rest through tool search or on-demand loading, merge overlapping tools, rewrite descriptions to say when to use each, move procedures into skills, and shorten tool results. Measure tool-selection accuracy before and after.

blocks.title: After a long session the agent "forgot" the user said never to substitute brands. What went wrong and how do you prevent it?
blocks.text: Compaction or trimming dropped the constraint. Keep durable user constraints in a pinned section or structured state that is re-injected after every compaction, have the summary prompt explicitly preserve constraints, and test with a long-session eval that checks early instructions late in the run.

modules.title: M8 · Evals: measuring quality
modules.summary: The journey gave you one eval harness and a regression gate. This module is the full discipline: where test cases come from, how to grade what has no single right answer, and how to trust the grader.

blocks.text: A golden dataset is a versioned set of inputs with expected outputs or pass criteria that defines "working" for your feature.
How it behaves

Build it from real usage and real failures, not imagination: common requests, edge cases, adversarial inputs and every bug you fix. Fifty well-chosen cases beat a thousand generic ones. Keep a held-out slice you never tune against, record why each case exists, and grow it whenever production surprises you.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Tuning the prompt against the whole set. You then measure how well you memorised it.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: production logs + bug reports + edge cases → label expected result → version in repo → split dev / held-out → grow with each failure

blocks.title: How would you build the first eval set for a brand-new feature with no users?
blocks.text: Write 30 to 50 cases by hand across the request types and risks you expect, add synthetic variations, and have a domain person review them. Replace and extend with real traffic and real failures as soon as there is any.
Error analysis is reading a sample of real outputs, writing down what is wrong with each in your own words, then grouping those notes into failure categories and counting them.
How it behaves

It comes before choosing metrics. The counted categories tell you what to fix first and which evaluators are worth building. It is the highest-value hour in AI engineering and it is manual: 50 to 100 traces, open notes first, categories second. Repeat after each significant change.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Adopting generic metrics from a library before looking at a single output. You measure what is easy, not what is broken.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: sample 50–100 traces → read each, free-text note → group notes into categories → count → fix the biggest → repeat

blocks.title: What is the first thing you do when asked to "improve the quality" of an LLM feature?
blocks.text: Read real outputs. Sample traces, annotate what is wrong, cluster into failure modes and count them. That tells you whether the problem is retrieval, the prompt, the tool, or the data, before spending effort on any one of them.
An LLM judge is a model prompted to grade another model's output against criteria. It scales grading of things with no exact answer, such as tone, completeness or groundedness.
How it behaves

Make each judge narrow: one criterion, a binary pass/fail, the reasoning written before the verdict, and a few labelled examples. Then validate it against human labels and report agreement; an unvalidated judge is an opinion. Known biases include favouring longer answers, position effects and leniency towards its own style. Prefer code checks wherever a check can be written.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: One judge prompt returning a 1–10 "quality" score. Nobody can say what a 7 means, and it drifts.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: input + output + criterion → judge model: reasoning then pass/fail → compare with human labels → agreement good? use → poor? fix judge prompt

blocks.title: How do you know whether to trust an LLM judge?
blocks.text: Have humans label a sample, run the judge on the same items, and measure agreement, including true-positive and true-negative rates separately. Iterate on the judge prompt until agreement is acceptable, and re-check whenever the judge model changes.
Pairwise evaluation shows a grader two outputs for the same input and asks which is better. Relative judgments are more consistent than absolute scores, for humans and models alike.
How it behaves

Randomise which side each version appears on to cancel position bias, allow ties, and report a win rate with enough cases to be meaningful. It is ideal for "is prompt B better than prompt A?" It does not tell you whether either is good enough, so pair it with absolute checks.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Always showing the new version second. The judge's position preference becomes your "improvement".

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: same input → output A, output B → shuffle sides → grader picks A, B or tie → win rate over many cases

blocks.title: When do you use pairwise comparison instead of scoring each output?
blocks.text: When comparing two versions of a prompt or model on subjective quality. Graders agree far more on "which is better" than on absolute scores. Use absolute pass/fail checks for release criteria.
A rubric spells out what each grade means with concrete descriptions and examples, so different graders give the same grade.
How it behaves

Split quality into separate criteria and grade each on its own, preferably pass/fail or a short scale with a definition per level. Write the rubric after error analysis so it targets real failures. The same rubric serves human labellers and the judge prompt.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: A scale with labels but no definitions ("3 = average"). Every grader fills in their own meaning.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: criteria from error analysis → define each level with an example → graders apply per criterion → check graders agree → refine wording

blocks.title: What makes a rubric good?
blocks.text: Criteria that are separate and specific, levels defined by observable features with examples, and evidence that two graders applying it reach the same result. Vague or combined criteria produce noise.
Faithfulness (groundedness) asks whether every claim in the answer is supported by the context that was provided. It is the direct measure of hallucination in RAG.
How it behaves

Method: break the answer into individual claims, check each against the retrieved context, score supported ÷ total. It says nothing about whether the context itself is correct or whether the answer addresses the question; an answer can be fully faithful and useless.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Scoring faithfulness against the model's general knowledge instead of the supplied context.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: answer → split into claims → each claim entailed by retrieved context? → supported ÷ total claims

blocks.title: An answer scores 100% faithful but the user is unhappy. How is that possible?
blocks.text: Faithfulness only checks that claims are supported by the context. The answer may not address the question, the retrieved context may be the wrong or outdated document, or it may be incomplete. Check answer relevance and retrieval quality too.
Answer relevance asks whether the response addresses what the user asked, without padding or drifting to something adjacent.
How it behaves

Judge it from the question and the answer alone. One automated approach generates the questions the answer would be a good reply to and compares them with the real question. Low relevance with high faithfulness usually means the retriever fetched an adjacent topic and the model dutifully summarised it.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Assuming a grounded answer is a relevant one.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: question + answer → judge: does the answer address this question directly and completely? → pass / fail with reason

blocks.title: How do faithfulness and answer relevance differ?
blocks.text: Faithfulness compares the answer to the context: is it supported? Relevance compares the answer to the question: does it address it? You need both, and they fail for different reasons.
Context precision asks how much of what you retrieved is relevant, and whether the relevant parts are ranked first. Its partner, context recall, asks whether everything needed was retrieved.
How it behaves

Low precision means noise in the prompt: more cost, and the model distracted by near-misses. Together the four RAG metrics localise a failure: context recall and precision grade the retriever; faithfulness and answer relevance grade the generator.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Raising k to improve recall and not noticing precision collapse and answers getting worse.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: retrieved chunks in rank order → label each relevant or not → precision weighted by rank → average over questions

blocks.title: Map the four standard RAG metrics to the component each one diagnoses.
blocks.text: Context recall and context precision evaluate retrieval: did we get what was needed, and how clean and well-ordered was it. Faithfulness and answer relevance evaluate generation: is the answer supported, and does it address the question.
Tool call accuracy checks whether the agent chose the right tool with the right arguments for a given input.
How it behaves

Because calls are structured, most of this is plain code: expected tool name, argument match (exact for ids, tolerant for free text), no forbidden tool called, valid schema. Cover the "no tool needed" case and the "must ask a clarifying question" case, since over-calling is as common as mis-calling.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Only testing cases where a tool should be called. The agent that calls a tool for "thanks!" passes everything.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: test input → agent's first tool call → compare name + arguments with expected → also check: should it have called nothing?

blocks.title: How do you evaluate whether an agent uses its tools correctly?
blocks.text: With labelled cases stating the expected tool and arguments, including cases where no tool or a clarifying question is correct. Compare in code, and track selection accuracy and argument accuracy separately.
A trajectory is the full sequence of steps an agent took. Trajectory evals grade the path as well as the result: required steps done, forbidden ones avoided, no wasted loops.
How it behaves

Grade the final state first (did the order actually get refunded in the test database), since there are usually many valid paths. Add path checks only where the path matters: "verified identity before refund", "never called delete", "under 10 steps". Run agents in a sandbox with a resettable environment, and run each case several times because agents are stochastic.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Demanding an exact step-by-step match. The eval breaks every time the agent finds a different valid route.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: task in sandbox → agent runs → check end state → check required / forbidden steps → count steps and cost → repeat N times

blocks.title: Why is checking only the final answer insufficient for agents?
blocks.text: The agent can reach a right-looking answer by a wrong path: skipping a required verification, calling a dangerous tool, or spending ten times the budget. Check the outcome in the environment plus the specific path constraints that matter.
The eval suite runs automatically on every change to a prompt, model, tool or retriever, and the change is blocked if scores fall below a threshold.
How it behaves

Use tiers: a fast, cheap subset on every pull request and the full suite nightly or before release. Because outputs vary, run cases more than once and compare against the baseline with a tolerance instead of demanding equality. Cache model responses for unchanged inputs to keep cost down.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: A gate so flaky that the team learns to rerun until green, which makes it worthless.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: change to prompt / model / code → CI runs eval subset → compare with baseline ± tolerance → pass: merge → fail: block with failing cases

blocks.title: How do you gate on a non-deterministic system?
blocks.text: Compare aggregate scores against a baseline with a tolerance, run cases multiple times, keep deterministic code checks strict, and reserve judge-based checks for thresholds on rates. Report which cases regressed, not only the number.
An A/B test sends a share of live traffic to a new prompt or model and compares real outcomes with the current one.
How it behaves

Offline evals say whether a change is safe to try; only an online test says whether users are better off. Pick the success metric in advance (task completion, resolution without escalation, conversion, thumbs-down rate), assign users consistently, run long enough for significance, and watch guardrail metrics such as cost and latency.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Declaring a winner after one day and 200 conversations.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: offline evals pass → split users A / B → log outcomes with variant → enough samples? → compare metric + guardrails → ship or revert

blocks.title: Your offline evals improved but the online metric did not. What might explain it?
blocks.text: The eval set does not represent real traffic, the judged criterion is not what users care about, the change traded quality for latency, or the test lacked power. Sample the online conversations and redo error analysis.
Human labels are the ground truth that everything else, including LLM judges, is calibrated against.
How it behaves

Use people who know the domain, give them the rubric, have two label a shared sample and measure their agreement; disagreement means the rubric is unclear. Make labelling fast with a purpose-built view of the trace. A little regular labelling beats a large one-off effort.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Outsourcing labels to people who do not know what a correct answer looks like in your domain.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: sample traces → domain expert labels with rubric → second labeller on overlap → measure agreement → resolve and refine rubric

blocks.title: Why not replace human labelling entirely with an LLM judge?
blocks.text: The judge needs a reference to be validated against, and its errors and biases are invisible without one. Humans define what good means; the judge extends their labels at scale and must be re-checked periodically.
Synthetic test data is model-generated inputs used to fill gaps: before launch, for rare cases, or for adversarial attempts.
How it behaves

Generate along explicit dimensions (user type × intent × difficulty × language) so coverage is deliberate, and seed it with real examples so it resembles users. Review a sample by hand. Generated questions tend to be cleaner and easier than real ones, so synthetic scores run optimistic.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Asking for "100 test questions" in one prompt and getting 100 variations of the same polite question.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: define dimensions → generate combinations → model writes realistic inputs per combination → human reviews a sample → add to dataset, tagged synthetic

blocks.title: What are the risks of evaluating only on synthetic data?
blocks.text: It under-represents the messiness of real users: typos, missing context, mixed languages, hostile input. Scores look better than production. Tag synthetic cases, keep them a minority once real data exists, and validate against real traffic.

lessons.title: Go deeper: an eval suite from nothing, in one week

blocks.text: Go deeper: an eval suite from nothing, in one week
Most teams know they should have evals and do not know where to start. The start is not a metric library. It is an afternoon of reading. This is the order that works, and each row is a section below.

rows: read 50 to 100 real traces and write a free-text note on each
a pile of observations in your own words
group the notes into failure categories and count them
a ranked list of what is actually wrong
for each top category, write the cheapest check that detects it
code checks, plus a short list that needs a judge
write one narrow judge per remaining criterion and compare it with your own labels
wire the checks into CI with a baseline and a per-category report

blocks.text: After that week the suite grows by one rule: every production failure becomes a case.
Error analysis, done once on paper
Thirty traces from the returns assistant (a real pass reads 50 to 100), each with the reviewer's note and, in a second pass, a category.

blocks.code:
# Error analysis: free-text notes on real traces -> categories -> counts. The counts decide what to fix first.
from collections import Counter

notes = [   # (trace id, what the reviewer wrote, category assigned in a second pass; None = the answer was fine)
    ("t01", "fine", None), ("t02", "quoted the 7-day rule for milk; dairy is 24h", "wrong policy section retrieved"),
    ("t03", "fine", None), ("t04", "table of delivery fees came out as one line of numbers", "table parsed badly"),
    ("t05", "said refund in 2 days, source says 5", "unsupported claim"), ("t06", "fine", None),
    ("t07", "follow-up 'and frozen?' answered about produce", "follow-up lost its subject"),
    ("t08", "fine", None), ("t09", "packaged-goods rule used for frozen peas", "wrong policy section retrieved"),
    ("t10", "fine", None), ("t11", "fee table again, wrong fee quoted", "table parsed badly"),
    ("t12", "asked for user id although logged in", "ignored tool instructions"), ("t13", "fine", None),
    ("t14", "clearance rule missed, said returnable", "wrong policy section retrieved"), ("t15", "fine", None),
    ("t16", "'what about that one' -> unrelated answer", "follow-up lost its subject"), ("t17", "fine", None),
    ("t18", "produce rule quoted for dairy", "wrong policy section retrieved"), ("t19", "fine", None),
    ("t20", "invented a 50 rupee coupon", "unsupported claim"), ("t21", "fine", None),
    ("t22", "fee table, third time", "table parsed badly"), ("t23", "fine", None), ("t24", "fine", None),
    ("t25", "frozen answered with packaged rule", "wrong policy section retrieved"), ("t26", "fine", None),
    ("t27", "fine", None), ("t28", "'is it the same?' -> generic answer", "follow-up lost its subject"),
    ("t29", "fine", None), ("t30", "fine", None),
]
bad = [c for _, _, c in notes if c]
print(f"{len(notes)} traces read, {len(bad)} with a problem ({len(bad) / len(notes):.0%})\n")
running = 0
print(f"{'failure category':34} count  share  cumulative")
for cat, n in Counter(bad).most_common():
    running += n
    print(f"{cat:34} {n:>5}  {n / len(bad):>5.0%}  {running / len(bad):>9.0%}")
print("\nTwo categories are over half the failures, and both sit in ingestion and retrieval, not in the prompt.")
print("A single 'quality score' of 53% would have said none of this.")
blocks.caption: From notes to a ranked list of failure categories

blocks.text: Nearly half the answers had a problem, which sounds like a prompt in need of rewriting. The counts say otherwise: the largest category is the wrong policy section being retrieved, and the next is a table that was parsed into a line of numbers. Rewriting the prompt would have fixed at most three of fourteen failures. This is why error analysis comes before everything else in the module, and why it is done by a person who knows what a right answer looks like.
Choose the cheapest evaluator that can see the failure

rows: Output is not valid JSON, a field is missing
Wrong tool, wrong arguments, a tool called when none was needed
Citation points to a chunk that does not contain the quote
Answer exceeds a length, uses a forbidden phrase, leaks an id
Claim not supported by the context
Answer does not address the question
Tone is wrong for the brand
LLM judge with examples, or pairwise
Is this actually the right medical, legal or financial answer?

blocks.text: Reach for a judge last. Every judge is a second model that can be wrong, costs money on each run, and has to be re-validated when it changes.
A judge you can defend
A judge that returns "quality: 7" tells you nothing you can act on. A usable judge checks one thing, explains before it decides, and returns pass or fail.

blocks.code:
You are checking one thing: whether every factual claim in the ANSWER
is supported by the CONTEXT. Ignore style, tone and completeness.

<context>
{the retrieved passages}
</context>
<answer>
{the assistant's answer}
</answer>

First list each factual claim in the answer and, beside it, the exact
sentence from the context that supports it, or "no support".
Then give the verdict on the last line as exactly PASS or FAIL.
FAIL if any claim has no support, including numbers and time limits.

Example of FAIL: the answer says "refunds take 2 days" and the context
says "within five working days".

blocks.text: Before trusting it, label answers yourself until you have at least thirty real failures as well as plenty of passes, oversampling the ones you suspect, run the judge on the same set, and look at two numbers separately: of the answers you failed, how many did the judge fail, and of the answers you passed, how many did it pass. The `judge_agreement.py` example earlier in this module computes exactly these. A judge that agrees 90% overall can still miss a third of the real failures, because failures are the minority. With only a handful of failures, that recall figure is itself very uncertain.
A suite that reports by category
The total is the least useful number an eval suite produces. This runner evaluates two prompt versions on ten cases with code checks and reports per category, then lists exactly which cases changed.

blocks.code:
# A small eval runner: code checks per case, results by category, and which cases changed between two versions.
import json

CASES = [   # id, category, what a correct output must satisfy
    {"id": "fmt-1", "cat": "format", "must": {"json": True}},
    {"id": "fmt-2", "cat": "format", "must": {"json": True}},
    {"id": "cite-1", "cat": "grounding", "must": {"cites": "policy#dairy"}},
    {"id": "cite-2", "cat": "grounding", "must": {"cites": "policy#refunds"}},
    {"id": "cite-3", "cat": "grounding", "must": {"cites": "policy#clearance"}},
    {"id": "tool-1", "cat": "tool use", "must": {"tool": "get_order"}},
    {"id": "tool-2", "cat": "tool use", "must": {"tool": None}},            # "thanks!" -> no tool should be called
    {"id": "tool-3", "cat": "tool use", "must": {"tool": "search_policy"}},
    {"id": "safe-1", "cat": "safety", "must": {"refuses": True}},           # asks for another customer's order
    {"id": "safe-2", "cat": "safety", "must": {"refuses": True}},           # injected instruction in a review
]
OUT = {     # scripted outputs of two prompt versions on the same cases
    "v7": {"fmt-1": '{"a":1}', "fmt-2": '{"a":2}', "cite-1": "policy#dairy", "cite-2": "policy#refunds", "cite-3": "policy#returns",
           "tool-1": "get_order", "tool-2": "get_order", "tool-3": "search_policy", "safe-1": "REFUSE", "safe-2": "REFUSE"},
    "v8": {"fmt-1": '{"a":1}', "fmt-2": '{"a":2}', "cite-1": "policy#dairy", "cite-2": "policy#refunds", "cite-3": "policy#clearance",
           "tool-1": "get_order", "tool-2": None, "tool-3": "search_policy", "safe-1": "REFUSE", "safe-2": "sent the email"},
}


def passed(case, out):
    must = case["must"]
    if "json" in must:
        try: json.loads(out); return True
        except (TypeError, ValueError): return False
    if "cites" in must: return out == must["cites"]
    if "tool" in must: return out == must["tool"]
    if "refuses" in must: return out == "REFUSE"


res = {v: {c["id"]: passed(c, OUT[v][c["id"]]) for c in CASES} for v in OUT}
print(f"{'category':12} {'v7':>6} {'v8':>6}")
for cat in dict.fromkeys(c["cat"] for c in CASES):
    ids = [c["id"] for c in CASES if c["cat"] == cat]
    print(f"{cat:12} " + " ".join(f"{sum(res[v][i] for i in ids)}/{len(ids):<4}" for v in OUT))
print(f"{'TOTAL':12} " + " ".join(f"{sum(res[v].values())}/{len(CASES):<3}" for v in OUT))
fixed = [i for i in res["v7"] if not res["v7"][i] and res["v8"][i]]
broke = [i for i in res["v7"] if res["v7"][i] and not res["v8"][i]]
print(f"\nfixed by v8: {fixed}\nbroken by v8: {broke}")
ABSOLUTE = ("safety", "format")                       # any failure in these categories blocks, new or old
hard = [c["id"] for c in CASES if c["cat"] in ABSOLUTE and not res["v8"][c["id"]]]
print("GATE:", f"BLOCK - {hard} failed, and safety and format cases must all pass whatever the total says" if hard else "pass")
blocks.caption: Two versions, four categories, and the cases that flipped

blocks.text: Version 8 scores higher overall, 9 of 10 against 8 of 10, and it must not ship: it fixed a citation and a needless tool call and broke a safety case, where an instruction planted in a product review was obeyed. A gate on the total would have waved it through. Gate per category, make safety and format cases absolute, and always print the cases that flipped.
Grading the path as well as the answer
For agents, the final message is not enough. This grader checks the end state in the test environment first, then a small number of path rules, across six runs of the same task.

blocks.code:
# Grading an agent run: the end state first, then only the path rules that matter, over several runs.
RULES = {"required_before": ("get_order", "issue_refund"),      # must look at the order before refunding
         "forbidden": {"delete_order", "run_sql"}, "max_steps": 6}


def grade(run):
    steps, state = run["steps"], run["end_state"]
    problems = []
    if state.get("refund") != 68:
        problems.append(f"end state: refund is {state.get('refund')}, expected 68")
    first, then = RULES["required_before"]
    if then in steps and (first not in steps or steps.index(first) > steps.index(then)):
        problems.append(f"path: {then} happened without {first} first")
    used = RULES["forbidden"] & set(steps)
    if used:
        problems.append(f"path: forbidden tool {sorted(used)}")
    if len(steps) > RULES["max_steps"]:
        problems.append(f"budget: {len(steps)} steps, limit {RULES['max_steps']}")
    return problems


runs = [   # the same task run 6 times; agents are not deterministic
    {"steps": ["get_order", "search_policy", "issue_refund"], "end_state": {"refund": 68}},
    {"steps": ["search_policy", "get_order", "issue_refund"], "end_state": {"refund": 68}},          # different order, still valid
    {"steps": ["issue_refund"], "end_state": {"refund": 68}},                                         # right result, skipped the check
    {"steps": ["get_order", "search_policy", "search_policy", "search_policy", "search_policy", "search_policy", "issue_refund"], "end_state": {"refund": 68}},
    {"steps": ["get_order", "search_policy", "issue_refund"], "end_state": {"refund": 680}},          # wrong amount
    {"steps": ["get_order", "search_policy", "issue_refund"], "end_state": {"refund": 68}},
]
ok = 0
for i, run in enumerate(runs, start=1):
    problems = grade(run)
    ok += not problems
    print(f"run {i}: {'PASS' if not problems else 'FAIL  ' + '; '.join(problems)}")
print(f"\npass rate {ok}/{len(runs)} = {ok / len(runs):.0%}")
print("Runs 1 and 2 took different paths and both pass: the grader checks outcomes and rules, not an exact script.")
print("Run 3 would pass a final-answer check. Only the path rule catches a refund issued without looking at the order.")
blocks.caption: Outcome, required order, forbidden tools and a step budget

blocks.text: Two different orderings both pass, so the grader is not a brittle script match. The third run issued the correct refund and produced a correct final answer, and still fails, because it refunded without ever looking at the order. And the pass rate is reported over several runs, because an agent that succeeds three times in six is a different product from one that succeeds six in six.
What a golden set should contain

rows: long inputs, mixed language, typos, follow-ups
things it must decline or hand off
a fifth of the total, across all of the above
chosen at random and left alone

blocks.text: What people get wrong about this module

items: "We will add evals once the product is stable." Without them you cannot tell whether it is.
"Pick a metrics library first." Generic metrics measure what is easy. Your failure categories tell you what to measure.
"The judge said 4.3 out of 5." An averaged score with no definition cannot be acted on. Use pass or fail on one criterion.
"The judge is a strong model, so it is right." Unvalidated, it is a confident opinion. Check it against human labels.
"The suite passed, so the release is good." It passed the cases you have. Production feedback is how the set learns the cases you lack.
"Agents cannot be tested because they are random." Check the end state and the path rules, and report a pass rate over several runs.

blocks.text: Practice: five problems

blocks.title: On 100 human-labelled answers, 20 are real failures. The judge fails 14 of those 20 and also fails 4 of the 80 good answers. What are its overall agreement, its recall on failures, and its false-alarm rate, and is it ready?
blocks.text: It agrees on 14 + 76 = 90 of 100, so 90% agreement. Recall on failures is 14 ÷ 20 = 70%. False alarms are 4 ÷ 80 = 5%. It is not ready as a release gate: it misses 30% of real failures. The 90% headline is carried by the easy majority of good answers.

blocks.title: A CI eval has 20 judge-scored cases and each one, with no real change, passes 95% of the time. The gate requires all 20 to pass. How often does the gate fail for no reason, and how do you fix it?
blocks.text: All pass with probability 0.95²⁰ = 0.36, so the gate goes red 64% of the time with nothing wrong, and people learn to ignore it. Gate on a rate with a tolerance against the baseline, run flaky cases more than once and take the majority, and keep the all-must-pass rule for deterministic code checks.

blocks.title: A pairwise judge prefers whichever answer is shown second 60% of the time when the two are equally good. Version B is always shown second and wins 60% of comparisons. What have you learned, and how do you design the comparison properly?
blocks.text: Nothing about B: 60% is exactly the position bias. Randomise which side each version appears on, or run every pair in both orders, so the bias cancels. With sides balanced, equal versions come out at 50%, and any remaining gap is a real preference.

blocks.title: Your thumbs-down rate is 4% and you hope a new prompt reduces it to 3%. Roughly how many conversations per variant does an A/B test need, using n ≈ 16 × p × (1 − p) ÷ d²?
blocks.text: p is about 0.035 and d is 0.01: 16 × 0.035 × 0.965 ÷ 0.0001 ≈ 5,400 conversations per variant. A few hundred conversations cannot detect a one-point change, which is why a result declared after a day is usually noise.

blocks.title: You have one day to give an existing RAG assistant its first evals. What do you build, in order?
blocks.text: Read 40 recent traces and tag failures. Turn the top two categories into checks: for retrieval failures, a small golden set of questions with the passages that answer them and recall@k; for grounding, the quote-in-chunk citation check. Add format and refusal cases as code checks. Run the set against the current version to record a baseline, and add the script to CI to report per category. The validated judge comes in week two.
Your eval plan
The build step asks for the assistant's suite. Fill this in first; it is also what you show in an interview when asked how you know the system works.

rows: from your own error analysis, dated
size, slices, where cases come from, the held-out slice
one criterion each, the prompt, the model, and its measured agreement with your labels
end-state assertions, path rules, runs per case
absolute categories, tolerance for the rest, what the report prints
fast subset on every change, full suite nightly, re-validation of judges when the judge model changes
how a production failure becomes a new case, and who does it

lessons.title: Evals: measuring quality: build and practise

blocks.text: Build the assistant's eval suite: a 60-case golden set from real failure categories, a calibrated LLM judge for faithfulness, a tool-call accuracy check for the agent, and a CI gate that blocks a change which fails any safety or format case, or drops a quality rate beyond a set tolerance.
Does the LLM judge agree with humans? Agreement rate and Cohen's kappa by hand

blocks.code:
# Is the LLM judge trustworthy? Compare its pass/fail verdicts with human labels on the same 20 answers.
human = "P P P F P F F P P P F P P F P P P F P P".split()
judge = "P P P F P P F P P P F P P P P P P F P P".split()

n = len(human)
agree = sum(h == j for h, j in zip(human, judge))
tp = sum(h == "F" and j == "F" for h, j in zip(human, judge))     # judge caught a real failure
fn = sum(h == "F" and j == "P" for h, j in zip(human, judge))     # judge missed a real failure
fp = sum(h == "P" and j == "F" for h, j in zip(human, judge))
tn = n - tp - fn - fp

p_observed = agree / n
p_h_fail, p_j_fail = human.count("F") / n, judge.count("F") / n
p_chance = p_h_fail * p_j_fail + (1 - p_h_fail) * (1 - p_j_fail)
kappa = (p_observed - p_chance) / (1 - p_chance)

print(f"raw agreement      {p_observed:.0%}  ({agree}/{n})")
print(f"agreement by chance {p_chance:.0%}")
print(f"Cohen's kappa      {kappa:.2f}")
print(f"failures caught    {tp}/{tp + fn}  (recall on failures {tp / (tp + fn):.0%})")
print(f"false alarms       {fp}/{fp + tn}")
print("verdict:", "judge misses real failures - fix its prompt before trusting it" if tp / (tp + fn) < 0.9 else "usable")
blocks.caption: judge_agreement.py

blocks.title: Design the evaluation strategy for the returns-policy RAG assistant.
blocks.text: Start with error analysis on real or pilot conversations. Build a golden set with questions, the passages that answer them and reference answers. Retrieval: recall@k, nDCG. Generation: faithfulness and answer relevance by a validated judge, citation validity by code. Add refusal cases for out-of-scope questions. Gate CI on a fast subset, run the full suite nightly, and feed production thumbs-down and escalations back into the set.

blocks.title: The team reports "quality is 4.2 out of 5" every week and nothing improves. What is wrong with this setup?
blocks.text: A single averaged score hides what is failing and cannot guide a fix. Replace it with failure categories from error analysis, binary checks per category, and counts of each. Then the weekly report says "table questions fail 30% of the time", which someone can act on.

modules.title: M9 · Observing production
modules.summary: What you record from live traffic, and the two numbers every stakeholder asks about: how slow and how much.

blocks.text: A trace is the full record of one request as a tree of spans: each model call, retrieval, tool call and sub-agent, with inputs, outputs, timing and token counts.
How it behaves

It answers "what did the model actually see and do" for any single bad answer, which logs of the final text cannot. Tag traces with user, session, prompt version and model so you can filter and compare. Traces are also the raw material for error analysis and for new eval cases.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Logging only the final answer. When it is wrong you cannot tell whether retrieval, a tool or the prompt caused it.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: request → root span → child spans: retrieve, model call, tool call, model call → each with input, output, tokens, latency → stored and searchable

blocks.title: A user reports a wrong answer from yesterday. What do you need to have recorded to debug it?
blocks.text: The trace: the exact prompt with system prompt version, retrieved chunks and scores, each tool call with arguments and result, model and parameters, outputs, token counts and timings, linked by a request id the user or support can quote.

Langfuse is an open-source LLM engineering platform: tracing, prompt management with versions, datasets and experiments, scores from judges, users and annotators, and cost dashboards. It can be self-hosted.
How it behaves

It is one of several tools in this category alongside LangSmith, Arize Phoenix, Braintrust and others. Choose on: open source and self-hosting, OpenTelemetry support, eval and annotation workflow, and how well it fits your stack. The category matters more than the brand; all of them rest on the same trace model.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Adopting a platform and never opening the traces. The tool does not do the error analysis for you.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: SDK or OTel instrumentation → traces + scores to platform → filter and inspect → add to dataset → run experiment → compare versions

blocks.title: What capabilities should an LLM observability platform provide?
blocks.text: Nested traces with token and cost data, prompt versioning linked to traces, datasets and experiment comparison, scoring from code, judges and humans, an annotation view, and export through open standards so you are not locked in.

OpenTelemetry (OTel) is the vendor-neutral standard for traces, metrics and logs. Its GenAI semantic conventions define standard attribute names for model calls, such as the model, token usage and operation.
How it behaves

Instrument once with OTel and send the data to any backend, including the APM your company already runs, so an LLM call appears as a span inside the same trace as the HTTP request and database query. The GenAI conventions are still maturing, so pin versions. Capturing prompt and response content is opt-in because of privacy.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Instrumenting with one vendor's proprietary SDK everywhere, then being unable to change vendor or join LLM spans to the rest of the request.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: app + LLM library instrumentation → OTel spans with gen_ai.* attributes → collector → any backend (APM or LLM platform)

blocks.title: Why use OpenTelemetry for LLM tracing instead of a vendor SDK?
blocks.text: It is a common standard: one instrumentation, any backend, and LLM spans join the existing distributed trace so you see the model call in context with the rest of the request. It avoids lock-in.
P95 latency is the time within which 95% of requests finish. One in twenty is slower. It describes the experience of your unluckiest regular users, which the average hides.
How it behaves

LLM latency has a long tail from output length, retries, cold caches and provider load. Track time to first token and total time separately, per model and per route. Set objectives on percentiles (p95, p99), and remember an agent's latency is the sum of its steps.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Reporting a 2-second average while p95 is 14 seconds and those users are leaving.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: collect latency per request → sort → value at 95th percentile → alert on p95 and p99, split by route and model

blocks.title: Why monitor p95 instead of mean latency?
blocks.text: Latency is skewed: the mean blends a few very slow requests into one number that describes no user and cannot say how many were slow. Percentiles show the tail directly. For a multi-step agent the tail compounds, so p95 per step matters even more.
