blocks.text: Say these numbers out loud in an interview, with their assumptions. Being roughly right in two minutes is the skill.
The gateway: one place for the decisions
Every model call from every team goes through one service. It is the natural home for everything in this module.

rows: apps name a task, not a vendor model
a model change is an app release
picks the model per request by rule or classifier
everything goes to the most expensive model
retry, another region, another model, degraded reply
a provider incident is your incident
per-user and per-tenant token budgets; interactive ahead of batch

blocks.text: Routing, with quality in the picture
The lab in this module showed what routing saves. This simulation adds the other axis: what it does to accuracy, under stated assumptions about how good each model is on easy and hard requests.

blocks.caption: Five strategies compared on cost and accuracy over 20,000 simulated requests

blocks.text: Sending everything to the small model is cheap and loses twelve points of accuracy. A router alone or a cascade alone each recover most of that. Combining them matches the large model at under half the cost here. Every one of those figures comes from the assumptions at the top of the file, which is the real lesson: a routing design is only as good as your measurements of each model on each kind of request, and those come from the eval suite.
One limit, two kinds of work
Provider capacity is a shared resource. This hour-long simulation gives a backfill job and live users the same token-per-minute limit, under two policies.

blocks.code:
# One provider rate limit, two kinds of work. What reserving capacity for interactive traffic changes.
import random

random.seed(2)
LIMIT = 100_000                # tokens per minute from the provider
MINUTES = 60
interactive = [random.randint(20_000, 60_000) if 15 <= m < 45 else random.randint(8_000, 20_000) for m in range(MINUTES)]
BATCH_BACKLOG = 4_500_000      # a backfill job with this many tokens to process


def simulate(policy):
    backlog, rejected, done_at = BATCH_BACKLOG, 0, None
    for m, need in enumerate(interactive):
        if policy == "first come":                           # the batch job grabs what it can, first
            batch = min(backlog, LIMIT)
            room = LIMIT - batch
        else:                                                # interactive first; batch takes what is left
            room = LIMIT
            batch = 0
        served = min(need, room)
        rejected += need - served
        if policy != "first come":
            batch = min(backlog, LIMIT - served)
        backlog -= batch
        if backlog == 0 and done_at is None:
            done_at = m + 1
    return rejected, done_at, backlog


total = sum(interactive)
print(f"interactive demand over the hour: {total:,} tokens, peak minute {max(interactive):,} of a {LIMIT:,} limit\n")
for policy in ("first come", "interactive first"):
    rejected, done_at, left = simulate(policy)
    finish = f"batch done at minute {done_at}" if done_at else f"batch has {left:,} tokens left after the hour"
    print(f"{policy:18} interactive tokens refused: {rejected:>9,} ({rejected / total:.0%})   {finish}")
print("\nSame limit, same work. Priority costs the batch job some minutes and costs the users nothing.")
blocks.caption: First come first served, against interactive-first with batch taking what is left

blocks.text: Without priority, the backfill takes the limit for 45 minutes and users are refused 86% of their tokens. With interactive traffic served first, users lose nothing and the job finishes slightly after the hour. Nothing was added except an ordering rule. Better still, move the backfill to a batch API with its own quota and a lower price.
Four caches, four different promises

blocks.text: A two-second budget, spent

rows: run in parallel; fast reranker over 40 candidates
skipped on first turns; small model otherwise
cached prefix, small fast model, low reasoning
output cap near 60 to 80 tokens at 80 to 100 tokens per second

blocks.text: An answer of 300 tokens cannot finish in two seconds at these speeds. Either the objective is on the first word, or the answer is short. Deciding which is a product decision; knowing that it must be decided is yours.
What people get wrong about this module

items: "Use the best model everywhere, optimise later." Later arrives with the first invoice. Route by measured need from the start.
"Fallbacks are configured." A fallback that has never served traffic will fail the first time it is needed.
"Semantic caching is free performance." It is the only cache here that can serve a wrong or someone else's answer.
"We are well under the rate limit." On average. Limits bite at the peak minute, and with the cache cold.
"Fine-tuning will teach it our data." It teaches behaviour. Facts belong in retrieval.
"The context window is large, so management is unnecessary." Cost and accuracy degrade long before the limit.

blocks.text: Practice: five problems

blocks.title: An app has 200,000 daily users; 15% use the assistant, sending 4 messages a day, each needing 1.6 model calls. The busiest minute is 5 times the average. How many model calls per minute at peak?
blocks.text: 200,000 × 0.15 × 4 × 1.6 = 192,000 calls a day. Divided by 1,440 minutes that is 133 a minute on average, and 667 at peak. Multiply by the tokens per call that count against your limit to compare with the provider's tokens per minute.

blocks.title: Each call has a 9,000-token prefix, 900 fresh input tokens and 220 output tokens. With 90% of prefixes cached, what counts against a limit that ignores cached input? What if the cache stops hitting? At 667 calls per minute, compare both with a 4,000,000 limit.
blocks.text: Cached: 900 + 900 + 220 = 2,020 tokens per call, 1.35 million per minute, about a third of the limit. Uncached: 9,000 + 900 + 220 = 10,120 per call, 6.75 million per minute, 169% of the limit. A broken prefix turns comfortable headroom into refusals at peak.

blocks.title: A small model answers easy requests correctly 96% of the time and hard ones 62%; a large model manages 98% and 93%. 65% of traffic is easy. What accuracy do all-small and all-large give, and what does that tell you about routing?
blocks.text: All-small: 0.65 × 0.96 + 0.35 × 0.62 = 0.841. All-large: 0.65 × 0.98 + 0.35 × 0.93 = 0.963. The whole gap comes from hard requests, where the small model loses 31 points; on easy ones it loses 2. So the saving is safe exactly where the router can identify easy requests, and a wrong "easy" label is expensive.

blocks.title: A nightly backfill and live chat share a 100,000 tokens-per-minute limit, and users are getting 429s whenever the job runs. Give three fixes in order of preference.
blocks.text: Move the backfill to the provider's batch API, which has separate quota and lower prices. If it must stay real-time, put both behind a limiter that serves interactive traffic first and gives the job only what is left. And schedule the job outside peak hours with its own cap, so even a limiter fault cannot starve users.

blocks.title: You must answer within two seconds at p95, and current answers average 300 tokens at 80 tokens per second. What do you tell the product team?
blocks.text: Generation alone takes 3.75 seconds, so the full answer cannot meet the target at this length. Offer the choice: make the objective time to first word, which streaming can hold near one second; or cap answers near 60 to 80 tokens; or use a faster model if evals allow. Then spend the remaining budget by running retrieval and guardrails in parallel and caching the prefix.
Your design document
The build step puts a gateway in front of the assistant. Write this page first; it is also the skeleton of a system-design interview answer.

blocks.title: Design an LLM gateway for a company with five product teams.
blocks.text: A single service all teams call, exposing a provider-neutral API. It handles authentication and per-team keys, routing and fallback rules, rate limiting with priorities and per-tenant quotas, prefix-friendly request shaping, response and semantic caches with scope keys, PII redaction, token and cost accounting per team and feature, tracing through OpenTelemetry, and budgets with alerts. Prompts and model choices are configuration with versions, so teams change them without redeploying.

blocks.title: The assistant must answer within 2 seconds p95. Where does the time go and what do you cut?
blocks.text: Budget: auth and guardrails ~100 ms, query rewrite, retrieval and rerank ~400 ms, model TTFT ~500 ms, then streaming. Run guardrails and retrieval in parallel, skip rewrite on first turns, use a fast reranker over fewer candidates, cache the prefix, use a small fast model with low reasoning, cap output, and stream so the first words appear inside the budget.

modules.title: M12 · Owning the model: tuning and serving
modules.summary: The journey trained a toy language model and named LoRA and quantization. Here is what those mean in practice, and what happens inside a GPU server when you stop renting an API.

blocks.text: LoRA (low-rank adaptation) freezes the model's weights and trains two small matrices beside each chosen layer. Their product is added to the frozen weight: W + B·A. You train well under 1% of the parameters.
How it behaves

Rank `r` sets capacity (commonly 8 to 64), `alpha` scales the update, and you choose which layers get adapters (attention projections at least). The result is a small adapter file you can swap per task or merge into the base for zero added latency. Data quality decides the outcome: hundreds to a few thousand clean, consistent examples, a held-out eval set, and a baseline from prompting to beat.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Fine-tuning before building an eval set. You cannot tell whether the tuned model is better, worse or merely different.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: base model (frozen) → add low-rank A and B to chosen layers → train only A, B on examples → evaluate vs baseline → ship adapter or merge

blocks.title: Why does LoRA work with so few trainable parameters?
blocks.text: The change needed to adapt a pretrained model to a task has low intrinsic rank, so it can be approximated by the product of two thin matrices. The base knowledge stays frozen and only the small update is learned.
QLoRA loads the frozen base model in 4-bit precision and trains LoRA adapters on top in higher precision. It makes fine-tuning a large model possible on a single consumer or mid-range GPU.
How it behaves

Gradients flow through the quantised weights into the adapters only. The usual recipe is 4-bit NF4 quantisation with double quantisation and a higher-precision compute type. Memory drops by several times. The QLoRA paper reports quality matching 16-bit fine-tuning and no loss of training speed in its tests; measure both on your own hardware and task.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Expecting it to speed up training. It saves memory, not time.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: load base in 4-bit (frozen) → attach LoRA adapters in 16-bit → train adapters → save adapter → use with quantised or full base

blocks.title: What does QLoRA add to LoRA?
blocks.text: Quantising the frozen base model to 4 bits during training, which cuts GPU memory enough to tune large models on modest hardware, with small quality loss. The trained artefact is still a LoRA adapter.
Quantization stores weights with fewer bits (8 or 4 instead of 16), shrinking the model and its memory use so it fits on cheaper hardware and runs faster where memory bandwidth is the limit.
How it behaves

Post-training quantisation needs no retraining. 8-bit is nearly lossless, 4-bit usually acceptable, below that quality falls quickly. Formats and methods include GGUF (llama.cpp, Ollama), AWQ and GPTQ. Always re-run your evals on the quantised model, because loss shows up unevenly: long reasoning, maths and rare languages degrade first.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Assuming a 4-bit model behaves like the original because a benchmark average moved by one point.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: 16-bit weights → map to 8- or 4-bit levels (with calibration) → smaller file, less memory → re-run evals → deploy

blocks.title: What do you trade when you quantise a model to 4 bits?
blocks.text: Memory and often speed are gained, roughly a quarter of the 16-bit size, at the cost of some accuracy that concentrates in harder tasks. Measure on your own eval set rather than relying on a headline benchmark.

Distillation trains a small "student" model to reproduce the behaviour of a large "teacher". For LLM applications that usually means generating outputs with the big model on your task and fine-tuning a small model on them.
How it behaves

It is how you turn an expensive prototype into a cheap, fast production model for one narrow, high-volume task. You need a large, representative set of inputs, filtering of the teacher's outputs with your evals, and a check that the student holds up on edge cases. Check the teacher provider's terms before training on its outputs.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Distilling a broad open-ended assistant. The student copies the easy cases and fails the long tail.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: real task inputs → teacher model produces outputs → filter with evals → fine-tune small student → eval vs teacher → route volume to student

blocks.title: When is distillation worth the effort?
blocks.text: When one narrow task runs at high volume and a large model does it well: classification, extraction, routing, a fixed-format rewrite. The student can cut cost and latency by an order of magnitude, with the large model kept as fallback.
Closed models are reached only through a provider's API. Open-weight models can be downloaded and run on your own hardware or through any host.
How it behaves

Closed: highest capability, no operations, pay per token, data leaves your boundary, versions are retired on the provider's schedule. Open: control over data, cost at scale, customisation and version pinning, but you carry serving, scaling, evaluation and safety, and top capability usually trails. "Open" varies: read the licence for commercial limits. Many teams run both behind a gateway.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Choosing self-hosting to "save money" at low volume, then paying for an idle GPU and an engineer to run it.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: need: top capability, low ops → closed API → need: data stays in-house, high volume, custom tuning → open weights → often both, behind one gateway

blocks.title: Give three reasons to self-host an open-weight model and three reasons not to.
blocks.text: For: data residency or privacy requirements, predictable cost at sustained high volume, full control of tuning and versions. Against: operational burden of GPUs and scaling, lower peak capability, and poor economics when traffic is low or bursty.
vLLM is an open-source inference server for running open-weight LLMs on GPUs with high throughput. It exposes an OpenAI-compatible HTTP API, so existing client code works by changing the base URL.
How it behaves

Its speed comes from continuous batching and PagedAttention, plus prefix caching, quantised model support, LoRA adapter serving and structured output. Alternatives include Hugging Face TGI, TensorRT-LLM, llama.cpp and Ollama for local use. Key settings: GPU memory fraction, maximum context length, and maximum concurrent sequences.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Serving with a plain Python loop around `model.generate`, handling one request at a time on a GPU that could serve dozens.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: client (OpenAI-compatible API) → vLLM scheduler → continuous batching on GPU → paged KV cache → streamed tokens back

blocks.title: Why use a dedicated inference server instead of calling the model from a web framework?
blocks.text: A dedicated engine batches requests dynamically, manages KV-cache memory efficiently, streams, and exposes metrics. A naive loop serves one request at a time and wastes most of the GPU.

A GPU processes many sequences in one forward pass. Continuous batching adds new requests to the running batch and removes finished ones at every token step, instead of waiting for a whole batch to finish.
How it behaves

With static batching, short requests wait for the longest one in their batch and new arrivals wait for the next batch. With continuous batching the GPU stays full and latency for short requests stays low. It is the single biggest throughput gain in LLM serving.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Benchmarking a server with one request at a time and concluding it is slow. Its strength appears under concurrency.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: batch running → each step: finished sequences leave, waiting requests join → GPU always full → no waiting for the slowest

blocks.title: How does continuous batching differ from static batching?
blocks.text: Static batching groups requests and runs them to completion together, so all wait for the longest. Continuous batching reshuffles membership every decoding step, admitting new requests as others finish, which raises throughput and cuts queueing delay.

PagedAttention, introduced by vLLM, stores each sequence's KV cache in fixed-size blocks allocated on demand, the way an operating system pages memory, instead of reserving one large contiguous region per request.
How it behaves

Reserving for the maximum length wastes most of the memory, which limits batch size. Paging removes that waste, so more sequences fit on the GPU, and blocks can be shared between sequences with a common prefix (copy-on-write), which is how prefix caching and parallel sampling become cheap.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Assuming every engine works this way. Engines that reserve the full context for each slot, such as llama.cpp and Ollama, lose concurrency as you raise the context length; with paged allocation only the tokens actually in use take memory.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: sequence grows → allocate next KV block on demand → block table maps logical → physical → shared prefix blocks reused across requests

blocks.title: What problem does PagedAttention solve?
blocks.text: KV-cache memory fragmentation and over-reservation. By allocating cache in small blocks as sequences grow and sharing blocks for common prefixes, it lets many more requests run concurrently on the same GPU.

A small, fast draft model proposes several next tokens; the large model checks them all in one parallel pass and keeps the drafted tokens it accepts. The output follows the same distribution as the large model's alone (token-for-token identical under greedy decoding), produced faster.
How it behaves

It works because verifying k tokens in parallel costs about one large-model step. The gain depends on how often the draft is right: high for predictable text and code, low for creative or difficult text, where it can even slow things down. Variants draft from the prompt itself (n-gram lookup) for tasks that copy input, such as code edits.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Pairing a draft model that disagrees most of the time; every rejected draft is wasted work.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: draft model proposes k tokens → large model verifies all k in one pass → accept matching prefix → large model supplies the next token → repeat

blocks.title: Does speculative decoding change the output quality?
blocks.text: No. Under greedy decoding the accepted tokens are exactly those the large model would have produced; with sampling, drafts are accepted or resampled in a way that preserves the large model's output distribution. Only speed changes, and the speed-up depends on the draft's acceptance rate.
Throughput is total tokens per second across all users. Latency is how long one user waits. Bigger batches raise throughput and, past a point, raise each user's latency.
How it behaves

Pick the operating point from the product: interactive chat is tuned to a latency objective (TTFT and tokens per second per user); offline jobs are tuned for throughput and cost per token. Load-test with realistic prompt and output lengths and a realistic arrival pattern, and read the curve of latency against concurrency to find the knee.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Quoting a server's maximum tokens per second as if every user would experience it.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: raise concurrency → throughput rises → per-request latency rises → find the knee → set max concurrency to meet the latency objective

blocks.title: How do you decide the maximum concurrency for a self-hosted model?
blocks.text: Load-test with production-like requests, plot p95 TTFT and per-user tokens per second against concurrency, and choose the highest concurrency that still meets the latency objective. Autoscale replicas beyond that point.
An API charges per token with nothing to run. A GPU charges per hour whether or not it is busy.
How it behaves

Break-even depends on utilisation: GPU cost per hour ÷ tokens actually served per hour, compared with the API price for a model of equal eval quality. Add the hidden costs: engineers on call, idle capacity for peaks and failover, evaluation and upgrades. Self-hosting wins with steady, high, predictable volume on a model small enough to serve efficiently; APIs win for spiky load, top-tier quality and small teams.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Comparing at 100% GPU utilisation. Real fleets sit far lower once peaks and redundancy are covered.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: GPU $/hour ÷ (tokens/sec × 3600 × utilisation) = $/token self-hosted → add ops cost → compare with API $/token at equal quality

blocks.title: How would you decide between a provider API and renting GPUs?
blocks.text: Confirm an open model meets the eval bar, load-test its tokens per second, estimate realistic utilisation, compute cost per token including redundancy and people, and compare with API pricing. Factor in data requirements and the team's ability to operate GPUs.

Every rung of this module costs more to operate than the one below. Climb only when a measurement says the rung you are on is not enough. Tool names and commands below were checked on 12 November 2026 against the PEFT, Ollama and vLLM documentation.

blocks.text: Most products never need to pass rung 2. Knowing the higher rungs still matters: it is how you tell when someone is proposing them too early.
LoRA, trained by hand

The topic said LoRA freezes the model and trains two thin matrices. This example does exactly that with plain Python lists: a frozen matrix `W`, a task that needs `W` plus a low-rank change, and gradient descent on `A` and `B` only.

blocks.code:
# LoRA trained by hand: the base matrix W never changes; only two thin matrices A and B learn the difference.
import random

random.seed(3)
D, R, ALPHA, LR, STEPS = 16, 2, 4, 0.004, 2000
SCALE = ALPHA / R                                           # the standard LoRA scaling factor
rnd = lambda: random.gauss(0, 1)
matvec = lambda M, v: [sum(m * x for m, x in zip(row, v)) for row in M]

W = [[rnd() * 0.5 for _ in range(D)] for _ in range(D)]     # pretrained weights: frozen
u = [[rnd() * 0.6 for _ in range(R)] for _ in range(D)]     # the task needs W plus a rank-2 change
v = [[rnd() * 0.6 for _ in range(D)] for _ in range(R)]
target = lambda x: [a + b for a, b in zip(matvec(W, x), matvec(u, matvec(v, x)))]
data = [[rnd() for _ in range(D)] for _ in range(48)]

A = [[rnd() * 0.1 for _ in range(D)] for _ in range(R)]     # R x D, small random start
B = [[0.0] * R for _ in range(D)]                           # D x R, zeros: training starts exactly at the base model
W_before = [row[:] for row in W]


def forward(x):
    ax = matvec(A, x)
    return [w + SCALE * b for w, b in zip(matvec(W, x), matvec(B, ax))], ax


def loss():
    return sum(sum((p - t) ** 2 for p, t in zip(forward(x)[0], target(x))) for x in data) / len(data)


print(f"trainable: A {R}x{D} + B {D}x{R} = {2 * D * R} numbers, instead of {D * D} for full fine-tuning ({2 * D * R / (D * D):.0%})")
print(f"at real model width 4096 and rank 16 the same idea trains {2 * 4096 * 16:,} numbers instead of {4096 * 4096:,} ({2 * 4096 * 16 / 4096 ** 2:.2%})")
print(f"step    0  loss {loss():.4f}   (B is zero, so this is the untouched base model)")
for step in range(1, STEPS + 1):
    x = random.choice(data)
    pred, ax = forward(x)
    err = [p - t for p, t in zip(pred, target(x))]
    bt_err = [sum(B[i][k] * err[i] for i in range(D)) for k in range(R)]
    for i in range(D):
        for k in range(R):
            B[i][k] -= LR * SCALE * err[i] * ax[k]
    for k in range(R):
        for j in range(D):
            A[k][j] -= LR * SCALE * bt_err[k] * x[j]
    if step in (50, 200, 2000):
        print(f"step {step:>4}  loss {loss():.4f}")

print("base weights changed during training:", W != W_before)
merged = [[W[i][j] + SCALE * sum(B[i][k] * A[k][j] for k in range(R)) for j in range(D)] for i in range(D)]
x = data[0]
gap = max(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(matvec(merged, x), forward(x)[0]))
print(f"after merging W + scale*B*A into one matrix, outputs differ by {"less than 1e-12" if gap < 1e-12 else format(gap, ".1e")}: same model, no extra latency")
blocks.caption: Frozen base, two small trainable matrices, then a merge

items: `B` starts at zero, so before any training the adapted model is exactly the base model. That is why LoRA training starts stable.
The loss falls to zero while the base weights never change.
After training, `W + scale × B × A` is folded into one matrix and gives the same outputs. A merged adapter adds no latency; an unmerged one can be swapped per request.
The scaling factor is `alpha ÷ rank`. In the PEFT library that is the default; a rank-stabilised option divides by the square root of the rank instead.

blocks.text: What the settings mean
These are the `LoraConfig` parameters you will actually change, with the library's current defaults.

blocks.text: Running a model on your own machine
Ollama is the quickest way to feel what an open model is like. It serves an OpenAI-compatible API locally, so your existing client code works by changing the base URL.

blocks.text: Use it for the build step: pull a small model, send it the same twenty prompts as your hosted model, and record tokens per second and where the answers differ.
What a serving engine does differently

vLLM is started with `vllm serve <model>` and exposes OpenAI-compatible endpoints including chat completions, completions, responses and embeddings. Its command-line reference lists `--gpu-memory-utilization` (the share of GPU memory the engine may use), `--max-model-len` (context length for prompt plus output), `--enable-prefix-caching`, and `--enable-lora` with `--lora-modules`; the server listens on port 8000 by default. A cap on concurrent sequences also exists; confirm its exact flag with `vllm serve --help` for your version. LoRA adapters can be loaded at runtime, which its documentation recommends only for local development.

blocks.code:
# Static batching versus continuous batching on one GPU. One step produces one token for every running sequence.
import random

random.seed(12)
BATCH = 4
requests = []
t = 0.0
for i in range(40):
    t += random.expovariate(1 / 6)                           # a new request about every 6 steps
    requests.append({"id": i, "arrive": t, "tokens": random.choice([10, 15, 20, 30, 120])})   # a few long answers


def static():
    """Take up to BATCH waiting requests, run them all to the end of the longest, then take the next batch."""
    clock, done, queue = 0.0, {}, sorted(requests, key=lambda r: r["arrive"])
    while queue:
        clock = max(clock, queue[0]["arrive"])
        batch = [r for r in queue if r["arrive"] <= clock][:BATCH]
        queue = [r for r in queue if r not in batch]
        length = max(r["tokens"] for r in batch)             # short requests wait for the longest one
        for r in batch:
            done[r["id"]] = clock + length
        clock += length
    return done


def continuous():
    """Every step: finished sequences leave, waiting requests join while there is room."""
    clock, done, running, queue = 0.0, {}, [], sorted(requests, key=lambda r: r["arrive"])
    while queue or running:
        while queue and queue[0]["arrive"] <= clock and len(running) < BATCH:
            r = queue.pop(0); running.append({"id": r["id"], "left": r["tokens"]})
        if not running:
            clock = queue[0]["arrive"]; continue
        clock += 1
        for s in running:
            s["left"] -= 1
        for s in [s for s in running if s["left"] == 0]:
            done[s["id"]] = clock; running.remove(s)
    return done


print(f"{len(requests)} requests, batch size {BATCH}, output lengths 10 to 120 tokens\n")
print(f"{'policy':12} {'mean latency':>13} {'p95 latency':>12} {'short requests (<=20 tokens), mean':>36} {'finished at':>12}")
for name, fn in (("static", static), ("continuous", continuous)):
    done = fn()
    lat = sorted(done[r["id"]] - r["arrive"] for r in requests)
    short = [done[r["id"]] - r["arrive"] for r in requests if r["tokens"] <= 20]
    print(f"{name:12} {sum(lat) / len(lat):>10.0f} steps {lat[int(0.95 * len(lat))]:>8.0f} steps {sum(short) / len(short):>30.0f} steps {max(done.values()):>10.0f}")
print("\nSame GPU, same requests. In a static batch a 10-token answer waits for the 120-token one beside it.")
blocks.caption: Forty requests on one GPU under static and continuous batching

blocks.text: Mean latency drops from 412 steps to 110, and short answers go from 395 to 86. Nothing got faster; the GPU simply stopped making a ten-token answer wait for a 120-token one. The whole run also finishes in about half the time, which is the throughput gain. This is why a serving engine matters more than raw hardware, and why benchmarking a server with one request at a time tells you almost nothing.
Rent a GPU or pay per token

blocks.code:
# Rent a GPU or pay per token? The answer is mostly the utilisation figure. All prices are placeholders.
GPU_PER_HOUR = 2.50            # one GPU instance
TOKENS_PER_SEC = 2500          # total output tokens/second the server sustains at your latency objective (load-tested)
API_PER_M_OUT = 2.00           # API price per million output tokens for a model of equal eval quality
OPS_PER_MONTH = 3000           # share of an engineer's time, monitoring, spare capacity

print(f"GPU ${GPU_PER_HOUR}/hour, {TOKENS_PER_SEC:,} tokens/s when busy, API ${API_PER_M_OUT} per million output tokens\n")
print("utilisation   self-hosted $/M tokens   vs API")
for util in (0.05, 0.15, 0.30, 0.60, 0.90):
    per_m = GPU_PER_HOUR / (TOKENS_PER_SEC * 3600 * util) * 1e6
    print(f"{util:>10.0%}   {per_m:>18.2f}   {'cheaper' if per_m < API_PER_M_OUT else 'dearer'} ({per_m / API_PER_M_OUT:.1f}x)")

breakeven_util = GPU_PER_HOUR / (TOKENS_PER_SEC * 3600 * API_PER_M_OUT / 1e6)
print(f"\nbreak-even utilisation on hardware alone: {breakeven_util:.0%}")
monthly_tokens = TOKENS_PER_SEC * 3600 * 24 * 30 * 0.30
gpu_month = GPU_PER_HOUR * 24 * 30 * 2 + OPS_PER_MONTH       # two instances for redundancy, plus people
print(f"at 30% utilisation: {monthly_tokens / 1e9:.1f}B tokens/month; API ${monthly_tokens / 1e6 * API_PER_M_OUT:,.0f}, "
      f"self-hosted ${gpu_month:,.0f} with a second instance and operations")
print("The hardware comparison says self-host. Redundancy and people move the line, and low or spiky traffic moves it further.")
blocks.caption: Cost per million tokens at five utilisation levels, then the costs the hardware figure leaves out

blocks.text: On hardware alone, the GPU wins above 14% utilisation in this example. Add a second instance for redundancy and a share of an engineer, and at 30% utilisation the self-hosted option costs more than the API. Three things move the line: how busy the GPU really is across a whole day, whether an open model actually meets your eval bar, and what your team's time costs. Work it out with your own load-test figures before anyone orders hardware.
Shrinking a model: what each method buys

The quantization and format rows were checked on 12 November 2026 against the Hugging Face bitsandbytes and GGUF documentation, Ollama's import guide and the QLoRA paper. The distillation and speculative-decoding rows were checked against the papers that introduced them (Hinton and others, 2015; Leviathan and others, 2022) and vLLM's speculative decoding page. The note on provider terms was checked against Anthropic's commercial terms (section D.4); other providers' terms were not read. The memory figures are the documentation's, measured against the model's normal precision.

rows: halving memory with little quality loss
values far outside the usual range are where it loses accuracy; small models are more sensitive
weights in 4 bits, about a quarter of the memory
fitting a model on a small GPU or laptop
harder tasks degrade first; re-run evals
one binary file holding the weights and their metadata, at full precision or quantised
the level is in the file name (`Q4_K_M`, `Q8_0`): pick it deliberately. Ollama does not quantise a GGUF on import
train LoRA adapters through a frozen 4-bit base
it saves memory; only the adapters train. Use the NF4 data type for the base. The paper reports no loss of quality or training speed against 16-bit; confirm on your task
a small model is trained on a large one's outputs, so that one cheaper model is deployed
one narrow task at high volume

long-tail inputs; whether the teacher's provider permits it. Anthropic's commercial terms, for example, bar using the service to train competing AI models, so read your provider's terms before building a teacher pipeline
a small model drafts several tokens, the large one checks them in one parallel pass
faster output with the same output distribution, and no retraining
only helps when the draft is usually right. vLLM enables it with `--speculative-config` and describes the gain as lower latency at low to medium load, not at high load

blocks.text: What people get wrong about this module

items: "Fine-tuning will make it know our documents." It changes behaviour. Facts that change belong in retrieval.
"Open models are free." The weights are. The GPUs, the on-call and the upgrades are not.
"We need our own model for privacy." Check the provider's data terms and regional options first; that is usually a smaller project.
"Quantised models are the same but smaller." Usually close on easy tasks, measurably worse on hard ones.
"A bigger rank is a better adapter." Past what the task needs it only adds overfitting and file size.
"It ran on my laptop, so it will serve production." One user at a time is a different problem from two hundred.

blocks.text: Practice: five problems

blocks.title: A model has hidden width 4,096. You add LoRA adapters of rank 16 to 64 of its weight matrices. How many parameters are trained, and what fraction is that of an 8-billion-parameter model?
blocks.text: Each adapter is 2 × 4,096 × 16 = 131,072 parameters. Across 64 matrices that is 8,388,608, about 8.4 million. Divided by 8 billion that is 0.1%. At 16 bits each the adapter file is roughly 17 MB.

blocks.title: A GPU costs $2.50 an hour and sustains 2,500 output tokens per second when fully busy. An API of equal quality costs $2 per million output tokens. At what utilisation does the hardware alone break even, and why is that not the whole answer?
blocks.text: At full use the GPU produces 9 million tokens an hour, so $0.28 per million. Break-even is 0.28 ÷ 2 = 14% utilisation. It is not the whole answer because you need spare capacity for peaks, a second instance for failures, and people to run it; real fleets also sit idle at night.

blocks.title: Why does continuous batching lower latency for short requests without making the GPU any faster?
blocks.text: In a static batch every request waits until the longest one finishes, and new arrivals wait for the next batch. Continuous batching removes finished sequences and admits waiting ones at every token step, so a short request leaves as soon as it is done and its slot is reused immediately.

blocks.title: You fine-tuned a classifier and its accuracy on your test set rose from 88% to 97%. A colleague says the test set was sampled from the same file as the training data. What could be wrong, and how do you check?
blocks.text: If near-duplicates of training examples are in the test set, the score measures memorisation. Deduplicate across the two sets, including paraphrases, and hold out by source or time. Then evaluate on fresh production samples. Also confirm the 88% baseline used the same test set and a properly tuned prompt.

blocks.title: A product manager asks for "our own fine-tuned model" for the support assistant. What do you ask before agreeing?
blocks.text: What failure it should fix, and whether that failure is knowledge or behaviour. Whether an eval set exists and what the prompted baseline scores. Whether retrieval, better examples or a smaller hosted model were tried. How many reviewed examples exist. Who retrains it when the base model is retired or the policy changes. If the gap is knowledge, the answer is retrieval, not training.
Your model ownership sheet
The build step sizes a fine-tune on paper and runs a model locally. Record the result here; it is the evidence for staying on a rung or climbing.

rows: The task and the measured gap
eval score with the best prompt, and the score you need
examples, retrieval, a smaller or larger hosted model
size, source, who reviewed it, how the held-out set was separated
rank, alpha, target modules, and why
tuned score against baseline on the held-out set, plus regressions
model, quantisation, tokens per second on your machine, where answers differed
GPU memory for weights plus cache at your concurrency and context length
cost per million tokens at realistic utilisation, with redundancy and people
stay, or climb one rung, and the measurement that would change it

lessons.title: Owning the model: tuning and serving: build and practise

blocks.text: On paper first: size a LoRA fine-tune for the ticket classifier (parameters, data, eval). Then run a small open model locally with Ollama, measure tokens per second, and write the API-versus-GPU break-even for your traffic.
How few parameters LoRA trains, and what 8-bit and 4-bit rounding do to a weight matrix

blocks.code:
# LoRA parameter count, and what rounding weights to fewer bits does.
import random

d = 4096                                   # width of one attention projection matrix (d x d)
full = d * d
print(f"one {d}x{d} weight matrix: {full:,} parameters")
for r in (4, 16, 64):
    lora = 2 * d * r                       # A is r x d, B is d x r
    print(f"  LoRA rank {r:<3}: {lora:>9,} trainable  ({lora / full:.2%} of the matrix)")

layers, matrices = 32, 2                   # adapt 2 projections in each of 32 layers
print(f"whole model, rank 16 on {layers * matrices} matrices: {layers * matrices * 2 * d * 16 / 1e6:.1f}M trainable parameters")

random.seed(1)
weights = [random.gauss(0, 0.02) for _ in range(20000)]
lo, hi = min(weights), max(weights)


def quantize(ws, bits):
    levels = 2 ** bits - 1
    step = (hi - lo) / levels
    return [lo + round((w - lo) / step) * step for w in ws]


print("\nuniform quantization of 20,000 sample weights")
for bits in (8, 4, 2):
    q = quantize(weights, bits)
    err = sum(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(weights, q)) / len(weights)
    rel = err / (sum(abs(w) for w in weights) / len(weights))
    print(f"  {bits}-bit: {2 ** bits:>3} levels, mean error {rel:.1%} of a typical weight, size {bits * 100 / 16:g}% of 16-bit")

params_b = 8
for bits in (16, 8, 4):
    print(f"an {params_b}B-parameter model at {bits}-bit needs about {params_b * bits / 8:.0f} GB for weights alone")
blocks.caption: lora_math.py

blocks.title: A classification call runs 30 million times a month on a large hosted model and costs too much. Plan the migration to something cheaper.
blocks.text: Build the eval set first. Try a smaller hosted model with a tuned prompt and few-shot examples. If quality holds, switch with a cascade to the large model for low-confidence cases. If not, distil: label a large sample with the big model, filter, fine-tune a small model (LoRA), evaluate, and serve it hosted or on vLLM depending on break-even. Canary, compare online metrics, keep the large model as fallback.

blocks.title: A self-hosted model serves 4 requests per second with idle GPU utilisation shown at 30%. What is likely wrong?
blocks.text: Requests are probably processed one at a time or with small static batches, so the GPU waits between steps. Use an inference server with continuous batching, check maximum concurrent sequences and KV-cache memory settings, and confirm clients actually send requests concurrently.

modules.title: M13 · Ship and operate
modules.summary: Your DevOps Mastery Academy teaches Docker, Kubernetes, CI/CD and Terraform in depth. Each entry here is only what changes when the thing you deploy includes a prompt, a model and an index.

blocks.text: A container packages the service with its exact dependencies so it runs the same on a laptop, in CI and in production.
How it behaves

AI images go wrong on size and reproducibility. Pin Python and library versions (ML libraries break on minor bumps), use multi-stage builds, and keep model weights out of the image: mount or download them at start. GPU images need the matching CUDA base and the host's container runtime for GPUs.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Baking a multi-gigabyte model into the image, so every code change rebuilds and pushes gigabytes.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: pinned base image → install locked dependencies → copy code → weights mounted or fetched at start → run

blocks.title: Why keep model weights out of the container image?
blocks.text: Weights are large and change on a different schedule from code. Baking them in makes images huge, builds and deploys slow, and rollbacks heavy. Store them in a registry or object store and load at start or from a shared volume.
Compose starts several containers together from one file: the full stack on your machine.
How it behaves

A typical AI stack: API, worker, Postgres with pgvector, Redis, an observability tool, and optionally a local model server. It gives every developer and the CI job the same environment for integration tests and evals.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Developing against a shared cloud vector database, where one person's test wipes another's index.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: compose file → api + worker + postgres/pgvector + redis + tracing + (local model) → one command up → same stack in CI

blocks.title: What services would your docker-compose file contain for a RAG application?
blocks.text: The API, a background worker, Postgres with the vector extension, Redis for cache and queue, a tracing backend, and optionally a local model server for offline development, with health checks and seeded test data.
Kubernetes runs containers across machines: it schedules, restarts, scales and connects them.
How it behaves

AI specifics: GPU workloads set `nvidia.com/gpu` under resource limits (whole GPUs, with the NVIDIA device plugin on the node) and run on dedicated node pools; model pods take minutes to start because weights load, so readiness probes and startup budgets matter; streaming needs ingress timeouts raised and buffering off. Stateless API pods and stateful model servers are scaled by different rules.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Default 60-second idle timeouts cutting a response during a silent gap, such as a long tool call or reasoning before the first token. Send heartbeats or raise the timeout.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: deployment → pods on CPU pool (API) and GPU pool (model server) → service → ingress with streaming-friendly timeouts

blocks.title: What is different about running a model server on Kubernetes compared with a normal API?
blocks.text: It needs GPU resources and node pools, has long cold starts while weights load, holds large memory, scales on queue or concurrency instead of CPU, and needs longer timeouts and no response buffering for streaming.
Continuous integration builds and tests every change; continuous delivery ships what passes.
How it behaves

In AI systems a prompt edit, a model version bump, a retrieval setting and a tool description are all deployable changes with behavioural impact. They go through the same pipeline as code: review, automated evals, staged rollout. Nothing is edited live in a console.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Editing the production prompt in a dashboard with no review, test or history.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: change (code, prompt, model, index config) → build → unit tests → eval gate → deploy to staging → canary → full rollout

blocks.title: Which artefacts in an AI system must go through CI/CD?
blocks.text: Application code, prompts and few-shot examples, model identifiers and parameters, tool definitions, retrieval and chunking configuration, and guardrail rules. Each can change behaviour and each needs versioning, tests and a rollback path.
GitHub Actions runs workflows on repository events such as pull requests and merges.
How it behaves

An AI workflow adds an eval job: start the stack, run the eval subset, post a score comparison on the pull request, fail on regression. Keep provider keys in encrypted secrets, never expose them to workflows from forks, cap spend per run, and cache model responses for unchanged cases.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Running untrusted pull-request code in a workflow that holds secrets. The plain `pull_request` trigger gives pull requests from forks no secrets at all; the leak happens with `pull_request_target`, or a self-hosted runner, that checks out and runs the fork's code.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: pull request → workflow: lint + tests → start services → run eval subset → comment score diff → pass or fail

blocks.title: How do you run LLM evals in GitHub Actions safely and cheaply?
blocks.text: Store keys as secrets, keep the plain `pull_request` trigger so forks receive none, have a maintainer run evals for fork contributions, run a small fast subset on pull requests and the full suite on a schedule, cache responses keyed by prompt and model, and set a spend cap and timeouts.
An eval gate is a required check: the change cannot merge or deploy unless eval scores meet the bar.
How it behaves

Define it per metric: hard gates for deterministic checks and safety cases (must be 100%), tolerance bands for judge-scored quality compared with the main-branch baseline. Show the failing cases in the report. Keep the gate fast and stable, or people will route around it.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: A single averaged score as the gate; a severe regression in one category hides behind gains elsewhere.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: run evals on change → deterministic + safety checks: all pass? → quality metrics within tolerance of baseline? → allow or block with cases

blocks.title: What should an eval gate block on?
blocks.text: Any failure in safety, security or format checks, and any quality metric falling beyond a set tolerance from the baseline, evaluated per category rather than as one average. It should report exactly which cases regressed.
Configuration that differs between development, staging and production lives outside the code.
How it behaves

For AI: model identifier, prompt version, temperature, token limits, retrieval settings, feature flags, provider endpoints and keys. Pin exact dated model versions, never a floating "latest" alias, so staging and production run the same thing and a provider update cannot change behaviour unannounced.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Using a "latest" model alias in production and discovering a behaviour change from user complaints.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: config per environment → pinned model version + prompt version + limits + flags → loaded at start → logged with every request

blocks.title: Why pin a specific model version in configuration?
blocks.text: Aliases move when the provider releases a new version, changing behaviour without a deploy. Pinning makes behaviour reproducible, lets you evaluate an upgrade deliberately, and makes rollback a config change.
Infrastructure is defined in versioned files (Terraform, CloudFormation, Pulumi) and created by a tool, not by hand.
How it behaves

Include the AI pieces: model endpoints and provisioned capacity, vector database, GPU node pools, queues, buckets, IAM roles that scope which service may invoke which model, budgets and alarms. A reviewed plan before apply is the control against expensive mistakes.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: A GPU cluster created by hand for a test and found three weeks later on the invoice.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: code describes resources → plan (diff) → review → apply → state tracked → destroy when done

blocks.title: Which AI-specific resources belong in infrastructure as code?
blocks.text: Model access and endpoints, IAM policies limiting model invocation, vector stores, GPU node pools and autoscaling rules, queues and buckets for ingestion, secrets references, and cost budgets with alerts.
Functions run on demand and scale to zero, billed per invocation.
How it behaves

They suit API-calling AI backends and event-driven ingestion with spiky traffic. Limits to check: maximum execution time against long agent runs, response streaming support, cold starts adding to time to first token, payload size, and concurrency caps. They are not for hosting model weights.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: A long agent run killed by the function timeout at the 15-minute mark, with no checkpoint.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: event or HTTP → function (cold start?) → call model API → stream or return → scale to zero

blocks.title: When is serverless a good fit for an AI feature, and when is it not?
blocks.text: Good for bursty, short, API-backed requests and event-triggered pipelines. Poor for long-running agents, heavy in-process models, or strict latency targets hurt by cold starts, unless you add provisioned concurrency and checkpointing.
GPU instances are the machines that run open models. The number that matters first is GPU memory (VRAM), which decides which model at which precision and context length fits.
How it behaves

Rough sizing: parameters × bytes per weight (2 at 16-bit, ~0.5 at 4-bit) plus KV cache for your concurrency and context. Spot instances are cheap for batch and training but can be reclaimed. Capacity is often scarce, so reserve ahead. Scale-to-zero saves money and costs minutes of cold start.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Choosing by price and finding the model plus KV cache does not fit in memory at the context length you need.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: model size × precision = weight memory → + KV cache for concurrency × context → pick GPU with headroom → on-demand vs spot vs reserved

blocks.title: How do you estimate the GPU memory needed to serve a model?
blocks.text: Multiply parameter count by bytes per weight for the chosen precision to get weight memory, then add KV-cache memory for the expected concurrent sequences and context length, plus overhead. Validate with a load test.
Ollama downloads and runs open models on your own machine with one command and serves a local HTTP API, including an OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
How it behaves

It runs quantised GGUF models, so a laptop can run small and mid-size models. Use it for offline development, privacy-sensitive experiments, cheap CI for plumbing tests, and learning. It handles a few requests at once but is not a high-throughput engine: for concurrent production traffic use a batching server such as vLLM.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Load-testing Ollama and concluding open models are slow. It is not designed for many concurrent users.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: ollama pull model → local server on a port → app points its client at localhost → develop offline → swap base URL for production

blocks.title: Where does Ollama fit and where does it not?
blocks.text: It fits local development, prototyping, privacy-bound experiments and teaching. It does not fit high-concurrency production serving, where engines with continuous batching are needed.
Autoscaling adds or removes replicas as load changes.
How it behaves

CPU percentage is the wrong signal for AI. API tiers that mostly wait on a provider scale on concurrent requests; model servers scale on queue depth, in-flight sequences or tokens per second. GPU replicas take minutes to become ready, so keep a warm minimum, scale up early and down slowly. Your ceiling may be the provider's rate limit rather than your pods.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Scaling API pods to 50 and gaining nothing, because the provider's tokens-per-minute limit was the bottleneck.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: metric (queue depth, concurrency, tokens/sec) → above target? → add replica (minutes for GPU) → below for a while? → remove

blocks.title: What metric should autoscale a self-hosted model server?
blocks.text: Load-based signals such as queue length, concurrent sequences or time waiting in queue, not CPU. Combine with a warm minimum and conservative scale-down because cold starts are long.
A load balancer spreads requests across replicas.
How it behaves

LLM requests vary a thousand-fold in cost and last seconds to minutes, so round-robin overloads some replicas. Prefer least-in-flight or queue-aware routing. Streaming needs long-lived connections and no buffering. Routing a conversation to the replica that already holds its prefix in cache (prefix- or session-affinity) cuts time to first token.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Round-robin sending three huge requests to one replica while another idles.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: request → balancer picks least-loaded (or cache-affine) replica → long-lived streaming connection → replica health feeds back

blocks.title: Why is round-robin a poor fit for LLM serving?
blocks.text: Requests differ hugely in duration and token count, so equal counts do not mean equal load. Least-outstanding-requests or queue-aware balancing evens it out, and cache-aware routing improves latency.
A canary sends a small share of real traffic to the new version and compares it with the current one before widening.
How it behaves

For AI changes compare quality signals as well as errors: thumbs-down rate, escalations, retries, judge scores on sampled outputs, cost and latency per request. Shadow mode comes first when possible: run the new version on live inputs without showing its output. Widen in steps with automatic rollback rules.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Watching only HTTP errors. The new prompt returns 200 with worse answers.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: shadow run (no user impact) → 1–5% canary → compare quality + cost + latency vs control → widen in steps or roll back

blocks.title: What do you monitor during a canary of a new prompt?
blocks.text: Besides errors and latency: user feedback and retry rates, escalation or task-completion rate, sampled judge scores, refusal and format-failure rates, tokens and cost per request, each compared with the control group.
A feature flag switches behaviour at runtime without a deploy.
How it behaves

Flags select the model, prompt version or whole AI feature per user segment, drive A/B tests and gradual rollouts, and act as a kill switch that turns the feature off or to a safe fallback in seconds. Log the flag variant with every trace so outcomes can be compared.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: No kill switch. A misbehaving AI feature stays live for the hours an emergency release takes.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: request → flag service: user in which variant? → model + prompt for that variant → variant logged in trace → kill switch overrides

blocks.title: Why does every AI feature need a kill switch?
blocks.text: Failures can be behavioural, sudden and reputational: a provider change, an attack, a bad prompt. A flag lets you disable or downgrade the feature immediately without a release, limiting harm while you investigate.
Prompts are versioned artefacts with history, review and an id recorded on every request.
How it behaves

Keep them in the repository or a prompt registry, as templates with named variables, each change reviewed and run through evals. Store the version id in traces so any output can be tied to the exact prompt. A prompt is tied to a model: version them as a pair, since a prompt tuned for one model can underperform on another.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Prompt strings scattered through application code, edited ad hoc, with no way to tell which one produced a given answer.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: prompt template in repo or registry → change via review → evals → version id → deployed by config or flag → id in every trace

blocks.title: How do you find which prompt produced a bad answer from last Tuesday?
blocks.text: Every trace stores the prompt version id and model version. Look up the trace by request id, read the version, and fetch that exact template from the registry or repository history.
Record and pin which exact model produced every output, and manage upgrades as releases.
How it behaves

For hosted models pin dated identifiers, track deprecation dates, and plan migrations: run the eval suite on the new version, adjust prompts, canary. For your own models keep a registry (MLflow, Weights & Biases, or a cloud registry) holding weights, adapter, training data version, config and eval results, so any model can be reproduced and rolled back.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Learning a model is being retired from the error messages on its shutdown date.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: registry: model id + data version + config + eval scores → pinned in config → upgrade = eval → prompt tune → canary → deprecation calendar

blocks.title: A provider is retiring the model you depend on in 60 days. What is your plan?
blocks.text: Run the full eval suite on candidate replacements, adapt prompts where scores drop, check feature parity (tools, structured output, context size, price), canary the new pair, roll out behind a flag, and keep the old version until the new one meets the bar.
Liveness says the process is running; readiness says it can serve traffic.
How it behaves

A model server is not ready until weights are loaded and a warm-up generation succeeds. An API tier's readiness should cover its own dependencies but not hard-fail on the model provider, or a provider blip removes every pod at once. Add a periodic synthetic request that checks a known answer end to end.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: A readiness probe that calls the paid LLM API every five seconds from every pod.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: liveness: process alive → readiness: weights loaded + warm-up ok + dependencies reachable → synthetic end-to-end check on a schedule

blocks.title: What should readiness mean for a pod serving a local model?
blocks.text: The model weights are loaded into GPU memory, a warm-up inference has completed, and required dependencies respond. Until then the pod must not receive traffic.
Dashboards show the system's state; alerts page a person when something needs action.
How it behaves

AI signals beyond the usual: time to first token, tokens per second, tokens and cost per request, cache hit rate, 429 and fallback rates, guardrail trigger rate, format-failure and refusal rates, agent steps per task, and quality proxies such as thumbs-down and escalation. Alert on symptoms users feel and on spend anomalies. Prometheus and Grafana are the common open stack.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Alerting on everything. The cost-spike page is lost among forty noisy ones.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: metrics: latency, TTFT, tokens, cost, cache hits, 429s, fallbacks, guardrail hits, feedback → dashboards → few actionable alerts → runbook

blocks.title: Name five alerts you would set for a production LLM feature.
blocks.text: p95 latency or TTFT above target, error or 429 rate rising, fallback rate above normal, cost per hour or per tenant anomaly, and a quality proxy such as thumbs-down or format-failure rate crossing a threshold.
A rollback returns to the last known good version quickly.
How it behaves

An AI system has several things to roll back: code, prompt version, model version, index version and config. Each needs a previous version kept ready and a one-step switch. Indexes are the slow one, so keep the old index until the new one has proven itself (blue-green). Decide rollback triggers in advance and practise them.

blocks.title: Pitfall
blocks.text: Re-indexing in place with a new embedding model. The old index is gone, and rolling back means days of re-embedding.

blocks.title: Flow
blocks.text: trigger (quality or errors) → switch flag or config to previous prompt/model → repoint to old index → verify → investigate

blocks.title: Why is rolling back a RAG system harder than rolling back an API?
blocks.text: Behaviour depends on several versioned parts that must match: prompt, model, embedding model and index. Reverting code alone is not enough, and a rebuilt index cannot be restored instantly unless the previous one was kept alongside.

lessons.title: Go deeper: four kinds of change, one way to release them

blocks.text: Go deeper: four kinds of change, one way to release them

Your DevOps Academy teaches pipelines for code. An AI product has three more things that change behaviour without a line of code changing, and each needs the same discipline. This table is the module in one view.

headers: How it can go wrong silently
rows: a parser no longer matches the model's output
answers get worse, or a safety case breaks, with every status still 200
flag back to the previous version id
tone, format and tool use shift; a tuned prompt underperforms
full eval suite, then prompt adjustments
config back to the previous pinned id, with its prompt
retrieval quality changes for every question
recall and nDCG on the golden set
new index beside the old, flag to switch reads
flag back; the old index is still there

blocks.text: The YAML in this section was written for this page and checked by parsing it. Neither file has been run: Compose needs a container runtime and the workflow needs GitHub, and neither was available here. Treat both as a starting point and run them in your own repository.
The stack on one machine
The same services every developer, and the CI job, can start with one command.

blocks.code:
services:
  api:
    build: .
    env_file: [{ path: .env, required: false }]
    ports: ["8000:8000"]
    depends_on:
      db: { condition: service_healthy }
      redis: { condition: service_started }
  worker:
    build: .
    command: python -m app.worker
    env_file: [{ path: .env, required: false }]
    depends_on:
      db: { condition: service_healthy }
      redis: { condition: service_started }
  db:
    image: pgvector/pgvector:pg16
    environment: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dev-only }
    ports: ["5432:5432"]
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 10
    volumes: ["pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data"]
  redis:
    image: redis:7
    ports: ["6379:6379"]
volumes:
  pgdata:

blocks.text: Model weights are not in any image, and the provider key comes from `.env`, which is not committed. A local model server can be added as a fifth service for offline work.

items: `required: false` lets the file load on a CI runner where no `.env` exists; without it Compose refuses to start anything.
The database and Redis publish their ports so that tests running on the host, as in the workflow below, can reach them. This is for development only.
The image ships the pgvector extension but does not enable it. Your first migration still runs `CREATE EXTENSION vector`.

The eval gate as a workflow
This is the gate from Module 8, running on every pull request.

blocks.code:
name: evals
on:
  pull_request:

jobs:
  eval-gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - name: Fork pull requests get no key, so a maintainer runs the gate for them
        if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name != github.repository
        run: exit 1
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Take the baseline from the target branch, not from the pull request
        run: |
          git fetch --depth=1 origin "${{ github.base_ref }}"
          git show FETCH_HEAD:evals/baseline.json > "$RUNNER_TEMP/baseline.json"
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with: { python-version: "3.12" }
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: docker compose up -d --wait db redis
      - run: python evals/run.py --subset fast --baseline "$RUNNER_TEMP/baseline.json" --max-cost-usd 2
        env:
          MODEL_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.MODEL_API_KEY }}
      - if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: eval-report, path: evals/report.md }

Shadow first
Before any user sees a new version, run it on live inputs and throw its output away. This compares eight shadowed requests for a move to a smaller model.

blocks.code:
# Shadow mode: the candidate runs on live inputs, its output is recorded and never shown. Compare before any user sees it.
import json

live = [   # (request id, what the current version returned, what the shadow version returned, ms, ms, cost, cost)
    ("q1", '{"intent":"refund","order":"A17"}', '{"intent":"refund","order":"A17"}', 820, 610, 0.0041, 0.0019),
    ("q2", '{"intent":"status","order":"B02"}', '{"intent":"status","order":"B02"}', 790, 580, 0.0040, 0.0018),
    ("q3", '{"intent":"refund","order":"C33"}', '{"intent":"complaint","order":"C33"}', 910, 640, 0.0043, 0.0020),
    ("q4", '{"intent":"cancel","order":"D10"}', '{"intent":"cancel","order":"D10"}', 805, 600, 0.0040, 0.0019),
    ("q5", '{"intent":"status","order":"E77"}', '{"intent":"status","order":"E77"', 780, 590, 0.0039, 0.0018),
    ("q6", '{"intent":"other","order":null}', '{"intent":"other","order":null}', 760, 570, 0.0038, 0.0017),
    ("q7", '{"intent":"refund","order":"F05"}', '{"intent":"refund","order":"F05"}', 840, 620, 0.0041, 0.0019),
    ("q8", '{"intent":"status","order":"G21"}', '{"intent":"status","order":"G21"}', 800, 605, 0.0040, 0.0018),
]


def parse(text):
    try:
        return json.loads(text)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return None


same = broken = 0
differ = []
for rid, cur, shadow, *_ in live:
    a, b = parse(cur), parse(shadow)
    if b is None:
        broken += 1; differ.append((rid, "shadow output does not parse"))
    elif a == b:
        same += 1
    else:
        differ.append((rid, f"current {a['intent']!r} vs shadow {b['intent']!r}"))
n = len(live)
mean = lambda i: sum(r[i] for r in live) / n
print(f"requests shadowed {n}   identical {same} ({same / n:.0%})   unparseable {broken}")
print(f"latency {mean(3):.0f} ms -> {mean(4):.0f} ms   cost ${mean(5):.4f} -> ${mean(6):.4f} per request")
print("needs a human to look:")
for rid, why in differ:
    print(f"  {rid}: {why}")
ok = broken == 0
print("decision:", "start a 5% canary" if ok else "NOT ready for canary: fix the truncated output first (likely an output cap on the smaller model)")
blocks.caption: Agreement, parse failures, latency and cost, and the two requests a person should read

blocks.text: The candidate is faster and less than half the price, and it is not ready: one output was cut off mid-JSON, and one request was classified differently. Shadowing found both at no cost to any user. The disagreement is not automatically a regression; someone has to read it, because sometimes the new version is the one that is right.
A rollout that stays put
A percentage rollout must give each user the same version every time, keep early users in as the percentage grows, and obey a kill switch instantly.

blocks.code:
# A percentage rollout that is stable per user: hash the user id, compare with the ramp, honour a kill switch.
import hashlib


def bucket(user_id, flag):
    digest = hashlib.sha256(f"{flag}:{user_id}".encode()).hexdigest()
    return int(digest[:8], 16) % 100                    # 0..99, the same every time for this user and flag


def variant(user_id, flag, percent, kill=False):
    if kill:
        return "control"                                # the kill switch wins over everything
    return "new" if bucket(user_id, flag) < percent else "control"


users = [f"user{i}" for i in range(2000)]
FLAG = "assistant-prompt-v8"
previous = set()
for percent in (5, 25, 100):
    now = {u for u in users if variant(u, FLAG, percent) == "new"}
    print(f"ramp {percent:>3}%: {len(now):>4} of {len(users)} users on the new version; "
          f"everyone from the earlier step still included: {previous <= now}")
    previous = now

u = "user42"
print(f"\n{u} is in bucket {bucket(u, FLAG)}: at 5% -> {variant(u, FLAG, 5)}, at 25% -> {variant(u, FLAG, 25)}, asked again -> {variant(u, FLAG, 25)}")
print(f"same user, a different flag: bucket {bucket(u, 'new-reranker')} (flags are independent, so one user is not always the guinea pig)")
print(f"kill switch on at 100%: {sum(variant(x, FLAG, 100, kill=True) == 'new' for x in users)} users on the new version")
blocks.caption: Hash the user id, ramp from 5% to 100%, then pull the switch

blocks.text: Hashing the flag name together with the user id is what makes assignment stable without storing anything, and what stops the same users from being first into every experiment. Log the variant on every trace, or the canary's metrics cannot be split.
Parts that must match
A release is a set of versions, and some of them only work in pairs. This check runs over a release and six possible rollbacks.

blocks.code:
# An AI release is several versioned parts that must match. Check a deployment, then check a rollback.
RELEASES = {
    "r41": {"code": "1.8.0", "prompt": "v7", "model": "model-large-2026-05", "embed": "embed-v2", "index": "idx-2026-10-01"},
    "r42": {"code": "1.9.0", "prompt": "v8", "model": "model-large-2026-09", "embed": "embed-v3", "index": "idx-2026-11-10"},
}
INDEX_BUILT_WITH = {"idx-2026-10-01": "embed-v2", "idx-2026-11-10": "embed-v3"}       # an index only works with its own embedding model
PROMPT_TUNED_FOR = {"v7": "model-large-2026-05", "v8": "model-large-2026-09"}          # each prompt was evaluated on one model
CODE_NEEDS_PROMPT = {"1.8.0": {"v7"}, "1.9.0": {"v7", "v8"}}                           # 1.9.0 can read both output formats


def problems(d):
    out = []
    if INDEX_BUILT_WITH[d["index"]] != d["embed"]:
        out.append(f"index {d['index']} was built with {INDEX_BUILT_WITH[d['index']]}, queries would use {d['embed']}: retrieval returns nonsense")
    if PROMPT_TUNED_FOR[d["prompt"]] != d["model"]:
        out.append(f"prompt {d['prompt']} was evaluated on {PROMPT_TUNED_FOR[d['prompt']]}, not {d['model']}: quality unknown")
    if d["prompt"] not in CODE_NEEDS_PROMPT[d["code"]]:
        out.append(f"code {d['code']} cannot parse the output of prompt {d['prompt']}")
    return out


def show(label, d):
    p = problems(d)
    print(f"{label:44} {'CONSISTENT' if not p else 'BROKEN'}")
    for line in p:
        print(f"    - {line}")


old, new = RELEASES["r41"], RELEASES["r42"]
show("r42 as released", new)
show("roll back the code only", {**new, "code": old["code"]})
show("roll back the model only", {**new, "model": old["model"]})
show("roll back the embedding model only", {**new, "embed": old["embed"]})
show("roll back prompt + model together", {**new, "prompt": old["prompt"], "model": old["model"]})
show("roll back embed + index together", {**new, "embed": old["embed"], "index": old["index"]})
show("roll back everything to r41", old)
print("\nRollback is by pair: prompt with model, embedding model with index. The old index must still exist to go back to.")
blocks.caption: Which partial rollbacks leave a working system

blocks.text: Rolling back one part alone breaks the system in three different ways: old code cannot parse the new prompt's output, the new prompt was never evaluated on the old model, and the new index is meaningless to the old embedding model. The safe moves are pairs: prompt with model, embedding model with index. And the second pair is only possible if the old index was kept. Record every release as a manifest of all five versions, and run a check like this before any rollback.
When a provider retires your model
Hosted models are retired on the provider's schedule. Treat it as a planned release, not an emergency.

blocks.text: What people get wrong about this module

items: "It is only a prompt change." It is a behaviour change to every request, shipped with no compiler to object.
"We can always roll back." Only the parts you kept, and only in the pairs that match.
"Status codes are green, so the release is fine." A worse answer returns 200.
"The canary looked fine after an hour." Quality signals are slow and noisy; decide the sample size first.
"Latest is the best model." A floating alias is an unreviewed release on someone else's schedule.
"We will re-index in place." Then there is no way back, and for hours the index is half one thing and half another.

blocks.text: Practice: five problems

blocks.title: Release r42 changed the prompt, the model version, the embedding model and the index. Quality dropped and you suspect retrieval. Which parts do you roll back, and what must be true for that to be possible?
blocks.text: Roll back the embedding model and the index together, since an index only works with the model that built it. That is possible only if the previous index was kept beside the new one. Leave the prompt and model on r42 if their evals are healthy, and confirm the combination with the retrieval metrics.

blocks.title: Why hash the flag name together with the user id for a percentage rollout, and not use a random number per request?
blocks.text: A per-request random number would flip a user between versions mid-conversation and make metrics impossible to attribute. Hashing the user id gives each user a fixed bucket, so they stay on one version and remain included as the percentage grows. Including the flag name gives different buckets per flag, so the same people are not always the first exposed.

blocks.title: A shadow run of a cheaper model shows 75% identical outputs, one unparseable output in eight, and half the cost. Do you start the canary?
blocks.text: No. A parse failure in one of eight would be a visible breakage at scale; find its cause first, commonly an output cap or weaker format adherence, and fix it with a schema or a higher cap. Read the outputs that differ to judge whether they are worse, equal or better. Re-run the shadow, then start the canary.

blocks.title: You are changing the embedding model for a live index of two million chunks. Describe the release.
blocks.text: Build the new index beside the old one, writing new documents to both. Compare recall and nDCG on the golden set. Shadow live queries against the new index. Switch reads by flag for a small share of traffic, watching quality, latency and cost. Widen in steps. Keep the old index until the new one has held, then retire it. At every point, rollback is switching the flag.

blocks.title: Write the three conditions under which a canary of a new prompt is automatically rolled back, and the one condition under which it is held.
blocks.text: Roll back if a quality proxy such as thumbs-down or escalation rate exceeds the control by a set margin, if cost per task exceeds the control by a set margin, or if p95 latency does. Add any failure of a safety or format check as an immediate rollback. Hold at the current percentage, without deciding, while the canary has fewer samples than the number you fixed in advance.

The build step ships the assistant behind a flag with an eval gate. This is the page to have open on release day.
